name: @backendx/mcp

tools.name: authenticate
tools.description: Exchange a Google ID token for a BackendX API token, and report the account it belongs to and its legal-consent state. Obtain the token via: gcloud auth print-identity-token. This tool NEVER records a legal consent — accepting BackendX's terms is the human's own legal act. It only reads the state into legal: when legal.signed_up is false (a new account) or legal.blocking is true (a revised document is in effect), every other BackendX tool is refused with CONSENT_REQUIRED until the human accepts; follow legal_note and next_actions — get_legal_status to show the documents, then record_legal_consent after the human has read and accepted them. legal is null when the state could not be read; that is unknown, not clear. A brand-new Google account whose email the sign-up policy does not admit is refused with SIGNUP_NOT_ELIGIBLE, and one that matches a Terms-of-Use restriction record (an account terminated for a violation cannot sign up again for a year) with SIGNUP_RESTRICTED — retrying changes neither. Account balances are not reported here and there is no account-level balance any more: what a project may do comes from its PLAN (get_plan), and the spendable unit is the project's AI tokens (get_plan requirements.tokens, get_token_ledger).

google_id_token.description: Google ID token from gcloud auth print-identity-token

tools.name: get_legal_status
tools.description: Read this account's legal-document state: one entry per document that applies (terms_of_use, privacy_policy, billing_policy, and dpa / github_addendum once they apply), each with action consent (the human must accept target_version), display (a notice to show — a minor change or a revision announced before it takes effect) or none. signed_up=false or blocking=true means every other BackendX tool is refused with CONSENT_REQUIRED until the human accepts; this tool and record_legal_consent are the way out and keep working while blocked. A consent is a legal act by the human: show the document first (include_text=true attaches the text of every document needing action; read_url is a browser link for the human), get their explicit acceptance, and only then call record_legal_consent. Pass doc_key (and optionally version) to fetch one document's text that the status does not list — the DPA for submit_deploy_questionnaire's dpa_acceptance (send the version shown here as dpa_version), or the GitHub addendum before manage_repo_access can join a repository. Document text is served without login.

include_text.description: Attach the Markdown text of target_version for every document whose action is not none. Default false — each document is thousands of tokens.

lang.description: Language of the document text and read_url (default en). Use the language the human will actually read: it is what record_legal_consent's langcode must state. A missing translation falls back to English and the text reports fallback=true.

doc_key.description: Fetch the text of this one document as requested_document, whether or not the status lists it. Known keys: terms_of_use, privacy_policy, billing_policy, dpa, github_addendum.

version.description: Version for doc_key: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, or "current" for the version in effect (the default). Use the version a 403 or a docs list named when there is one.

tools.name: record_legal_consent
tools.description: Record the human's acceptance (consented) or acknowledgement of a notice (acknowledged) of BackendX legal documents. THIS IS A LEGAL ACT BY THE HUMAN, not a setting: call it ONLY after you have shown them the document (get_legal_status with include_text=true, or its read_url) and they have explicitly accepted it in this conversation — never on their behalf, never to get past a CONSENT_REQUIRED error by yourself, and never with a version they were not shown. confirm=true is your statement that this happened. Use the target_version from get_legal_status (or the version a 403 named) and the language the human actually read. For a new account (get_legal_status signed_up=false) send a consented item for the CURRENT version of terms_of_use, privacy_policy and billing_policy together with the signup block. If you ask about marketing email, first say that it is sent through a mail delivery provider in the United States (privacy policy section 6) — see the marketing_email_agreed parameter. Before joining a GitHub repository (manage_repo_access) the GitHub addendum is recorded here with source github_delivery. The DPA is NOT recorded here — it is accepted per project via submit_deploy_questionnaire's dpa_acceptance. Recording is idempotent. If the document changed after it was shown, this answers LEGAL_VERSION_STALE: re-read get_legal_status, show the new version and ask again rather than just resending the new number. Returns the updated status, so get_legal_status need not be called again.

doc_key.description: Document key from get_legal_status (known: terms_of_use, privacy_policy, billing_policy, dpa, github_addendum).

version.description: The exact version the human was shown — target_version from get_legal_status, or the version a 403 named. Only the current or the upcoming version is accepted.

action.description: consented = the human accepted the document. acknowledged = the human saw a notice (action display) that needs no consent.

langcode.description: Language the human actually read ("en" or "ko"; the text's lang field). Recorded as evidence.

source.description: Why it is being recorded. Omit for the backend default (signup while signing up, reconsent for consented, notice for acknowledged). Use github_delivery for the GitHub addendum before joining a repository.

items.description: One entry per document the human accepted or acknowledged.

signup.description: Required exactly when get_legal_status reports signed_up=false (a new account); ignored by the backend otherwise. Must accompany consented items for the current version of all three platform documents.

adult_confirmed.description: The human's OWN confirmation that they are of legal age (Terms of Use §3.1). Must be true to sign up — ask them; never assume it.

marketing_email_agreed.description: true ONLY when the human explicitly opted in to marketing email. Optional; omitted means no. Before asking, tell the human: "The email is sent through a mail delivery provider in the United States." — and that the details (recipient, items, retention) are in section 6 of the privacy policy (get_legal_status read_url for privacy_policy, #section-6). That disclosure is part of the wording this opt-in is recorded against.

confirm.description: Must be true: your statement that the human was shown each document and explicitly accepted (or acknowledged) it in this conversation.

tools.name: get_account
tools.description: Get the authenticated BackendX account: which login providers are connected, and the intro/coupon flags that decide what a plan actually costs this user. This is the account axis, not the project axis — what a given project is allowed to do comes from its plan (get_plan), and this tool will not explain a refused action. There is NO account-level balance: the spendable unit is per-project AI tokens, whose balance is get_plan requirements.tokens and whose history is get_token_ledger. Use this before quoting a price: held_coupons and intro_free_months change the amount the user will be charged, and the list prices in get_plan_catalog do not account for them.

tools.name: get_consent_questions
tools.description: Fetch the consent questionnaire DEFINITION — the questions, their allowed option ids, and which ones block deployment. Needs no project and no authentication, so this is the only way to read the questions BEFORE create_project. Default stage="project_start" returns the items the web console asks before a project exists and records right after creating it — currently ONE item, restricted_services_ack (the user confirms the service is in none of the legally restricted categories); a project created through create_project starts without it, so show it to the user, collect a real answer, and submit it with submit_deploy_questionnaire before the first send_message. Items the definition still carries but no screen asks any more (presented=false — end_user_jurisdictions, minors_in_scope, age_gating_measures, sensitive_data_in_scope at the time of writing) are listed separately under not_asked: do NOT ask them — unanswered they do not block the deploy gate and the interview applies defaults, whereas an answer you record still counts, so a "yes" you collected would block managed deployment where a web-console user is never asked. These are legal disclosures recorded under the account owner's identity: never invent a value, never pick one on the user's behalf, and never soften a question. One caveat on wording: for restricted_services_ack the served title/description is a recording summary — the detailed statutory copy behind it (the full restricted-category definitions) is shown only in the web console and the Terms of Use, so if the user needs that detail before acknowledging, point them there instead of paraphrasing it. An option carrying blocking=true rules out BackendX-managed deployment for as long as it stands as the current answer, and the append-only audit trail keeps the row forever — warn the user before submitting it. Use stage="deploy" for the items the deploy wizard collects, or stage="all" for the whole definition (thousands of tokens; it lists not_presented ids instead of splitting them out). This returns the definition only; for a specific project's current answers, missing items and gate state use get_deploy_readiness.

lang.description: BCP-47 language for the question text (default: en). Unsupported values fall back to en. Ask in the language the user is speaking — they have to read and understand these before answering.

stage.description: Which collection point to return. "project_start" (default) = the items the web console asks before creating a project (currently restricted_services_ack only), which are injected into the interview. "deploy" = the items collected in the deploy wizard. Either way, items no screen asks (presented=false) come back under not_asked, not as questions. "all" = every item; only ask for it when you genuinely need the full definition, it is thousands of tokens.

tools.name: create_project
tools.description: Create a new BackendX project. Returns the project UUID for subsequent operations. Creating a project is free — there is no balance to check — but it is limited: creation is rate-limited per hour and per day (PROJECT_CREATE_RATE_LIMITED; paid-plan holders get a higher limit), and an account whose projects are all on the free Sandbox plan may own only a few projects that are still in the requirements interview at once (TOO_MANY_OPEN_PROJECTS until one of them moves on into the pipeline or is deleted — accounts with a paid-plan project have no such cap). So prefer continuing an unfinished project (list_projects) over starting a new one, and never create projects in a retry loop. What the project can DO afterwards comes from its plan (get_plan). Note what a project created here does NOT have: the web console asks one legal declaration BEFORE the project exists and records it the instant it is created — restricted_services_ack, the user's confirmation that the service is in none of the legally restricted categories — and a project created through this tool starts without it. Fetch its exact wording with get_consent_questions, put it to the user, and record it with submit_deploy_questionnaire BEFORE the first send_message: a recorded answer is injected into the interview as authoritative context, and the deploy gate requires it anyway. Do not ask the other legal items that definition still lists as not_asked (jurisdictions, minors, age gating, sensitive data): the web console no longer asks them, the interview applies defaults when they are unanswered and the deploy gate does not count them as missing — whereas a 'yes' you collected and recorded would rule out managed deployment. Check get_deploy_readiness to see where a project stands.

tools.name: send_message
tools.description: Send a message to the project's AI assistant and wait for the response. Handles all polling and retry logic internally. The AI typically asks 5-8 follow-up questions before starting the generation pipeline. Interview turns spend the project's AI tokens, and when the balance reaches zero the backend stops accepting them: this tool then fails with BUDGET_EXCEEDED and turn_stored=false, which means the message was NOT recorded and the assistant never saw it. That is not a transient error — re-sending the same text changes nothing until the balance is topped up (list_token_packs then purchase_tokens, or get_upgrade_url when the plan does not sell packs), after which the message has to be sent again. Check the balance with get_plan requirements.tokens before a long interview.

language.description: Only a HINT, sent as the message's language guess (en-US when omitted). The backend decides the conversation language itself: any Korean (Hangul) text in the message means ko-KR; otherwise the account's stored browser language when it is Korean or English; otherwise the request's country (Korea means ko-KR); only then this hint. So passing en-US does not make the interview English for an account the backend already associates with Korean. The language of the generated documents is fixed by the FIRST customer message of the project's first revision — write that first message in the language the user wants the deliverables in.

tools.name: get_project_status
tools.description: Get the current state of a project: pipeline stage, recent messages, provisioned artifacts, why it stopped if it did, and a summary of its subscription plan. Use this to check progress without sending a new message. READ failure_kind FIRST when something is not moving — it names the kind of stop, and the kinds need different tools. failure_kind="budget_exceeded" means the project ran out of AI tokens, not that anything broke: budget then carries the detail, budget_note says exactly what to do, and retry_pipeline is the WRONG answer there (the backend refuses it, and it would rebuild from scratch on a fresh meter and spend a second full budget for the same outcome). Which tool applies depends on budget.phase: "pipeline" means a run is halted mid-flight and resume_pipeline continues it from that point once the budget is raised, while "interview" means only the balance is empty — there is no halted run, the user's last message was NOT stored, and once tokens are available it simply gets sent again with send_message. Beware that in the interview case has_failed_stage reads true although no stage actually failed, so do not read it as a crash. Three failure_kind values hand the requirements back to the user instead — external_integration_unsupported, algorithm_infeasible and children_signin_conflict: BackendX reopens the interview by itself and explains why in an AI message, so read get_messages and answer with send_message (reopen_note says this; retry_pipeline is only the fallback when the reopen did not happen). Other failure_kind values (stage_failed, stage_stalled and the rest) are ordinary failures that retry_pipeline handles, and an unfamiliar value should be treated as one of those. waiting_for_frontend=true means the backend is BUILT and the pipeline is finishing the app's web frontend: workflow_state stays 6 and task_id is null during that phase, yet it is RUNNING, not stalled — progress_value then tracks the frontend run (0-100), and retry_pipeline would throw that work away. With failure_kind null, telling a project that is WAITING FOR THE USER from one that has STOPPED depends on the stage: in the requirements stage (workflow_state 0-1) both look identical from task_id alone, so has_failed_stage true with no task_id means the run hard-failed and needs retry_pipeline while false means the interview is waiting for an answer (send_message); from workflow_state 2 onwards has_failed_stage is not the test, and a missing task_id is itself the stall signal. Note that purchased_docs reports legacy per-artifact flags, not whether the plan grants anything — a false there does not mean the plan excludes it; and purchased_docs.source_repo now says only whether YOU (the caller) take part in the GitHub mirror, a pending invitation included — manage_repo_access(action:"status") gives the exact state. During the requirements interview interview_core_questions_remaining says how many core questions the user has not answered yet (0 means the interview is at its closing confirmation); it is null outside the interview. frontend summarises the web frontend BackendX generates for the backend (kind, live, url) — get_frontend_status has the detail. Once the project is complete (workflow_state 7) next_step names the next move: the BackendX-generated frontend first when there is one, then building your own client with get_api_clipboard (own_client_step). Call get_plan for what the plan actually allows and for the remaining allowances, and get_system_status when nothing starts at all.

tools.name: wait_for_pipeline
tools.description:
Wait for the generation pipeline to advance to the next stage or reach a target stage (default: 7 = ReadyToRun).
Returns immediately when a new stage is reached, so you can report progress to the user and call again.
Check target_reached in the response — if false, report the current stage and call this tool again.
While the target has not been reached the response also carries stage_average_minutes, the backend's measured average for the stage the project is currently in — use it to tell the user roughly how much longer to expect. It is omitted when there is no measurement for that stage, which is not an error.
This tool retries a stalled run by itself. When it does, auto_retry reports what came of it, and waiting_stopped=true means it gave up early for a reason waiting cannot fix: BackendX is in a maintenance hold (see get_system_status), the retry budget is spent and support has taken over, the retry restarted at the interview — which DISCARDS THE WRITTEN SRS and reopens the chat, so the project then needs the user to answer again with send_message — or the project ran out of AI tokens. That last one also sets budget_stopped=true with the budget detail, and it is the one case where looping is actively expensive: never answer it with retry_pipeline, because the backend refuses that and each attempt would rebuild from scratch on a fresh meter and spend another whole budget. Raise the budget first (purchase_tokens or get_upgrade_url) and then call resume_pipeline, or, when budget.phase is "interview", simply have the user send their message again. Read waiting_stopped_reason and relay it rather than calling this tool in a loop.
After the backend is built the pipeline also finishes the app's web frontend: the response then carries waiting_for_frontend=true with frontend_note, workflow_state stays 6 and progress_value tracks the frontend run (0-100). That phase is running, not stalled — keep calling this tool, never retry_pipeline; it has no measured duration, so no stage_average_minutes is given.
If workflow_state goes BACKWARDS (for example to 0), the pipeline stopped for a reason that hands the requirements back to the user and BackendX reopened the interview — interview_reopened_note says so; read get_messages and answer with send_message.

tools.name: retry_pipeline
tools.description: Retry a stalled or failed pipeline stage. Use it when get_project_status shows a project stopped with no task_id — during the requirements stage (workflow_state 0-1) that means has_failed_stage=true, and later it means the run is simply gone. CHECK failure_kind BEFORE CALLING: this tool is for ordinary stage faults only. If failure_kind is "budget_exceeded" the project ran out of AI tokens and the backend refuses this call outright, because a retry rotates the budget scope and rebuilds from the requirements document on a fresh meter — on an unchanged plan it halts in the same place and spends a whole budget again for nothing. The route there is to raise the budget (purchase_tokens or get_upgrade_url) and then resume_pipeline, which continues from exactly where the run stopped; in the interview phase there is no stopped run at all and the user just re-sends their message. Do not call it while get_project_status reports waiting_for_frontend=true either: the backend is built and the pipeline is finishing the app's web frontend with task_id null by design — it is running, and a retry accepted there would restart from the SRS, discard the frontend work and spend tokens again. For the stops that hand the requirements back to the user (failure_kind external_integration_unsupported, algorithm_infeasible, children_signin_conflict) BackendX reopens the interview by itself; this tool is only the fallback when that did not happen, and it then answers restart_point "interview". The backend decides where to restart and reports it as restart_point, and the two are NOT equivalent: srs_writer regenerates everything from the SRS down and queues a run, while interview means the fault was judged to be in the requirements, so the WRITTEN SRS IS CLEARED and the chat is reopened for the user to answer again — no run is queued and nothing waits for one. Read restart_point in the result before deciding what to do next, and tell the user when the SRS was discarded. The backend also caps retries per failure signature: once that is spent it answers human_review_required and a BackendX engineer takes over, so calling again does nothing. While the platform is draining for maintenance this is refused with MAINTENANCE_PENDING; that is an operational hold, not a fault in the project, and it clears by itself (see get_system_status).

tools.name: resume_pipeline
tools.description: Continue a generation pipeline that the backend stopped because the project ran out of its AI token budget. This is the ONLY way forward from that stop, and it is not interchangeable with retry_pipeline: resume keeps everything the run has produced — the workspace branch, the review ledger, the per-run counters and the same budget meter — and simply puts the stages that hard-failed back to pending before firing the pipeline again. retry_pipeline instead rotates the budget scope and rebuilds from the requirements document on a fresh meter, which on an unchanged plan stops at the same place and burns a whole cap a second time; the backend refuses it outright for a budget stop. Use this when get_project_status reports failure_kind="budget_exceeded" with budget.phase="pipeline", and only AFTER the budget has actually been raised — buy a token pack (list_token_packs, purchase_tokens) or move the plan up (get_upgrade_url), then call this. Calling it before that is refused with BUDGET_UPGRADE_REQUIRED and changes nothing. It does NOT apply when budget.phase is "interview": there is no stopped run to continue there, only an exhausted balance, so once tokens are available the user simply sends their message again with send_message — this tool checks that first and refuses with NOT_RESUMABLE_INTERVIEW_GATE rather than letting the backend answer with a code that reads like an ordinary failure. Follow an accepted resume with wait_for_pipeline.

tools.name: get_system_status
tools.description: Check whether the BackendX platform itself is healthy and whether a maintenance window is pending. Takes no arguments and needs no project — it is also the one tool that works before authenticate. Call it when pipeline work is not starting and you cannot tell whether the fault is the project or the platform: maintenance_pending=true means BackendX is draining for maintenance, so retry_pipeline is refused with MAINTENANCE_PENDING and the automatic run that normally follows a finished interview is held back. Nothing is broken and nothing is lost in that state — work already running finishes normally, and held work resumes on its own once maintenance completes, so the right response is to wait rather than to retry in a loop or change the project. When the operator has published an expected end time it comes back as maintenance_expected_end_at (UTC): pass it on to the user as the platform's own estimate. It is null when no window is pending or when the operator did not record one, and in that case say the end time is not published rather than guessing at one. The three component flags (celery, db, llm) are the platform's own health checks: a false there points at BackendX, not at the project, and the response deliberately carries no detail beyond the flag.

tools.name: list_projects
tools.description: List all projects for the authenticated user with their current states.

tools.name: get_plan_catalog
tools.description: Get the public catalogue of BackendX subscription plans: for each plan its code and display name, its rank, its monthly and yearly list prices with the currency, how many seats it includes and what an extra seat costs, which artifacts and capabilities it grants, and its operational limits. This is the ONLY authoritative source for what a plan costs — quote prices from here rather than from memory, and if the call fails, say the price could not be read instead of falling back to a figure you remember, because a stale number becomes a promise the invoice will not honour. It needs no project and no login, so it can answer a pricing question before the user has authenticated. Two fields decide whether a plan is reachable: self_serve=false means BackendX sells it through a conversation and change_plan will refuse it, and a null entry under prices means that plan is not sold on that billing interval in this environment. Use it together with get_plan, which reports what a particular project is on today, and get_upgrade_url, which is how a first paid subscription is actually started. Prices are minor units of the stated currency, so do not assume two decimal places, and note that they are list prices: a trial, an intro offer or a coupon on the account (get_account) changes what the user is actually charged, and preview_plan_change is what prices a specific move.

plan_code.description: Return only this plan. Omit to get the whole catalogue, which is usually what you want when comparing options for the user.

tools.name: get_pricing
tools.description: Get the LEGACY per-item price table (SRS, architecture, DB schema, dockerfiles, source repo, deployment, extra projects). Every entry is 0 under current pricing and none of them decides anything any more; the table is kept only so older clients do not break. THIS IS ALMOST CERTAINLY NOT THE TOOL YOU WANT. For what a subscription costs, call get_plan_catalog, which serves the authoritative plan list prices without needing a login. For what a particular project is on and what it may do, call get_plan. For what a specific plan change would charge, call preview_plan_change. Do not quote any number from this tool to the user as the price of anything.

tools.name: get_plan
tools.description: Get the project's subscription plan and what it grants: plan code, billing interval, status, period end, free-trial state, any scheduled plan change or cancellation, seat allowance, the project's AI TOKEN balance with current usage, the file-upload allowance, and the next invoice estimates. Read this BEFORE attempting a source download, a deployment, a requirement change or a file upload — all of those are gated by the project's PLAN. THE CONSUMABLE UNIT IS AI TOKENS, held per project, and there is no account-level balance of any kind. tokens is the honest breakdown and the only number to quote as a balance: monthly_free and monthly_remaining are the plan's monthly grant, purchased_remaining is what token packs added, initial_remaining is the one-off starter grant, and total_remaining is what the project can actually spend. The sibling keys included / additional / used are LEGACY NAMES kept for a UI transition — they now count tokens, not runs, so never present them as a number of requirement changes. can_purchase_tokens decides the remedy when the balance runs out: true means buy a pack (list_token_packs then purchase_tokens), false means the plan does not sell packs at all and only an upgrade helps (get_upgrade_url). get_token_ledger has the movement history; do not add the ledger up to get a balance, read it here. ALWAYS read is_trialing before any billing write: the backend folds a trialing subscription into status="active", so the trial is invisible in the raw plan, and while it is running a plan change is immediate, charged in full and destroys the trial. A cancellation is NOT changed by the trial: it is scheduled for the trial end, the trial keeps running until then, no plan fee is charged afterwards and it can be withdrawn. pending_state summarises what is queued: active (nothing), scheduled (plan.scheduled_change applies at rollover) or canceled (ends at current_period_end, next_invoice null) — change_plan, cancel_subscription and withdraw_scheduled_plan_change move between these. During a free trial, canceled means the cancellation lands at the trial end: is_trialing stays true until then and it can still be withdrawn. Two invoice estimates come back, not one: next_invoice is the BASE PLAN only, and seat_invoice is the separate monthly seat subscription that extra seats bill to, so the next month's total is the two added together. is_past_due=true (plan.status "past_due") means a payment FAILED and Stripe is retrying it: the project keeps its paid plan, and the fix is the billing portal (get_billing_portal_url) to update the card — never a new checkout through get_upgrade_url, which would open a second subscription; past_due_note spells it out. Amounts are Stripe minor units paired with a currency code; do not assume two decimal places. When the subscription bills in USD the response also carries indicative_unit_prices, the list prices for seats and for API-call, database and file-download overage — quote them as estimates and never for a subscription billed in another currency, where they are omitted precisely because a USD figure next to a non-USD bill is unreadable. Plan and token-pack prices are not guessed here: get_plan_catalog serves the authoritative plan list prices and list_token_packs the pack prices. See get_ops_usage for API-call and DB usage against the plan quota, and configure_hard_stop to cap API-call overage on a paid plan (on Sandbox it is always on). overage_note says what crossing a quota does on this plan: a paid plan bills the excess, while Sandbox bills nothing and blocks instead. accruing_overage lists the overage lines on the next invoice estimate — API calls, database and file downloads (transfer_overage).

tools.name: list_token_packs
tools.description: List the AI token packs that can be bought for a project, with their prices and the purchase terms that must be shown to the user first. AI tokens are what the interview and the generation pipeline spend: each project holds its own balance (get_plan requirements.tokens), and when it runs out the work stops until the balance is topped up or the plan is raised. Packs are the top-up route and purchase_tokens is the tool that buys one — call this first, because purchase_tokens deliberately does not repeat the prices and because the terms in this response are a legally required pre-purchase disclosure: show them to the user before asking for confirmation. The response carries packs (each with code, tokens, price_cents, currency and label), the unit these are counted in, max_quantity per purchase, validity_years, the refund window in days for ordinary and for EU/EEA customers, and terms. Prices come from the server on every call and are never cached here, so quote them from this response rather than from memory. Two things to get right when you present them: quote the pack total as a single number of tokens with no "bonus" split, because they are not sold that way, and do not convert tokens into a currency amount for the user. This tool needs no project and makes no charge.

tools.name: purchase_tokens
tools.description: Buy an AI token pack for a project. THE CARD IS CHARGED IMMEDIATELY: the backend raises a one-off invoice for the pack, pays it on the spot, and credits the tokens only once that payment succeeds — nothing is deferred to the next invoice. Call list_token_packs first and show the user the pack price and the purchase terms it returns; those terms are a legally required pre-purchase disclosure and this tool does not repeat them. Never pick the pack or the quantity yourself: ask the user which pack and how many, and read get_plan first so you know the current balance (requirements.tokens.total_remaining) and whether packs can be sold here at all — can_purchase_tokens is false on Sandbox and unsubscribed projects, where this call is refused and the only route is upgrading the plan (get_upgrade_url); it is also false while a failed subscription payment is being retried (get_plan is_past_due) — then the fix is updating the card in the billing portal (get_billing_portal_url), never a new checkout. THERE IS NO SELF-SERVICE REFUND: a withdrawal inside the cancellation window has to be requested from BackendX support by email, and only the unused portion is refundable, pro rata (together with the tax paid on that amount), with whatever is left of the pack cancelled. Say that before confirming rather than after. Purchased tokens expire five years from the purchase and are spent last, after the plan's monthly grant and the starter grant. Owner only, and you must pass confirm=true.

project_uuid.description: Project UUID the tokens are credited to

pack.description: Pack code, taken from the list_token_packs response. Do not guess it, and do not assume how many tokens a code carries — the catalogue is the source of that.

quantity.description: How many of this pack to buy (1-20, default 1). Every one of them is billed, so confirm the number with the user — there is no automatic bulk discount to make a larger number cheaper per token.

confirm.description: Must be true. This charges the project owner's card right now and cannot be undone from here.

tools.name: get_token_ledger
tools.description: Read a project's AI token movement history, newest first and paginated. Every row is one movement: kind tells you which, tokens is the signed amount (negative for spending, positive for a grant), srs_id ties it to a build where one applies, and meta carries a small per-kind detail. Spending kinds are interview_turn (an interview message) and pipeline_success (a completed generation run); granting kinds are initial (the one-off starter grant), purchase (a pack bought with purchase_tokens), conversion and manual (operator grants); refund is negative. THIS IS HISTORY, NOT A BALANCE — do not add the rows up to work out what is left, because the ledger is paginated and the balance is kept elsewhere. The balance is get_plan requirements.tokens, and total_remaining there is the only figure to quote. Use this to answer "where did the tokens go", to confirm a purchase actually landed, or to show the user what the build has cost so far. Reading it needs billing visibility on the project, which owners and admins have. No side effects and no charge.

tools.name: purchase_docs
tools.description: Check whether a project's plan grants each document type. Document access is granted by the project's PLAN, not bought per project — this tool only reports the verdict (already_owned / not_ready / plan_upgrade_required); there is nothing to buy and no balance to top up, and it never changes anything. "repo" reports whether the plan includes the GitHub source repository (plan_included; participation_state says where you stand — not_connected, eligible, invited or joined); opening it is a separate, per-member step done with manage_repo_access(action:"join"), which needs a linked GitHub account (link_github) and your acceptance of the GitHub addendum. Use "all" to check everything.

docs.description: Docs to check, or "all" for everything

tools.name: get_docs
tools.description: View project documentation. Free: api (HTTP endpoint reference), tasks (scheduled/worker job specs — check this one for batch or cron style apps), docker_images. Plan-gated: srs, architecture, db_schema, dockerfiles, repo (returns the GitHub URL — the URL alone does not grant access: each member joins the repository with manage_repo_access and accepts the GitHub invitation). A plan-gated doc comes back with purchased=false instead of content; purchase_docs reports whether the plan grants it. Note what doc="api" is for: reading or explaining the endpoints. If the goal is to BUILD a frontend or client app against this backend, call get_api_clipboard instead — it returns the same API surface wrapped in integration instructions (and, on request, the live base URL) as one ready-to-paste prompt.

doc.description: Document type to view: api, tasks, srs, architecture, db_schema, docker_images, dockerfiles, repo

revision.description: SRS revision (see list_revisions). Omit for the latest. Supported by api and tasks.

tools.name: get_er_diagram
tools.description: Get the entity-relationship diagram of this project's database schema, either as a picture for a person or as text you can read. format="mermaid" returns the diagram as Mermaid erDiagram source in the response — that is the form the backend added for agents, so use it when the goal is to reason about tables and relationships, and no output_directory is needed. That text is generated on demand from the schema rather than stored, so it can be unavailable (ERD_MERMAID_UNAVAILABLE) on a project whose images render fine; waiting does not fix that, and get_docs(doc="db_schema") is the way through. The image formats (svg, png, pdf, zip) are for handing a person a file: omit output_directory to get presigned download URLs plus metadata (they expire in about an hour), or pass output_directory to follow the redirect and save the file to disk. For the DDL itself rather than the relationships, get_docs with doc="db_schema" returns the statements the diagram is drawn from, behind the same plan gate. Multi-database projects render one diagram per database: the metadata response lists them in databases, and passing an unknown db comes back with the valid names.

output_directory.description: Directory to save the diagram file into. Omit to get presigned URLs and metadata instead of a file — or, with format="mermaid", to get the diagram text in the response.

format.description: Output format. "mermaid" returns Mermaid erDiagram TEXT in the response (and also writes it to disk if output_directory is given) — that is the one to use to read the schema. svg/png/pdf/zip are images for a person; zip bundles the rendered formats. Defaults to pdf when saving to disk, and is otherwise ignored by the metadata response, which always lists the svg/png/pdf URLs.

revision.description: SRS revision (see list_revisions). Omit for the latest revision.

db.description: Database name, for projects with more than one. Omit to get the first database by name. The valid names come back in the metadata response (databases) and in the error when an unknown one is passed.

tools.name: configure_environment
tools.description: View and optionally update a project's environment variables. Without overrides or reset_keys it just lists every configurable key with its state: must_fill (empty and required), optional_empty (empty but the service still runs), ready, or provided_by_backendx (deployment bucket only: BackendX fills the value at deploy time and does not show it, so the empty current_value is NOT a gap). Writing a value to, or resetting, a key of a BackendX-provided group switches the WHOLE group back to your own values — its other keys become unset unless you fill them too — so such writes are refused with BACKENDX_GROUP_OPT_OUT unless opt_out_backendx=true. The local and deployment buckets are SEPARATE stores — filling one does not fill the other, so populate type='deployment' before deploy_project even if the local run already works. Copy values across by reading one bucket and writing the other. Values are held in an encrypted secrets store, and this tool never echoes a value it did not just read. Writes run as reset_keys first, then overrides as one all-or-nothing batch, then a re-read: a failure part-way still reports reset_applied and overrides_applied, so read those rather than assuming nothing landed. Keys BackendX creates and uses on the project's behalf (such as BX_ADMIN_TOKEN) are not listed by default (include_readonly=true shows them as status read_only) and can never be written or reset — one in a batch makes the backend refuse the whole batch (READ_ONLY_KEY), which easily happens when re-writing values copied from a downloaded env.txt. On a refusal, only a 400 carries a usable explanation from the server; a permission refusal instead names a machine reason, and the two it distinguishes need different fixes — a role that lacks the capability (get_role_matrix says which role has it) versus a member holding the role but no seat (the owner has to free or buy one). Neither is fixed by retrying.

type.description: Which env bucket to read/write: 'local' (default) for local docker-compose runs via download_project, 'deployment' for managed-shared deploys via deploy_project.

revision.description: SRS revision (see list_revisions). Omit for the latest.

overrides.description: Environment variable values to set in the chosen bucket.

reset_keys.description: Keys whose user-supplied value should be cleared in the chosen bucket, falling back to the catalog default. Applied before overrides, so a key in both ends up with the new value.

include_readonly.description: Also list the keys BackendX creates and uses on the project's behalf (e.g. BX_ADMIN_TOKEN), as status read_only. Default false. They can be read but never written or reset.

opt_out_backendx.description: Deployment bucket only. Set true to confirm that writing or resetting a key of a BackendX-provided group (status provided_by_backendx) should switch that whole group back to your own values. Needed only when the tool refuses with BACKENDX_GROUP_OPT_OUT; ask the user first.

tools.name: download_project
tools.description: Download project files as a ZIP archive (docker-compose.yaml and config files) and optionally extract. Use get_docs to view documents separately. The ZIP is a snapshot taken at download time: a later requirement change or pipeline re-run does not update the extracted files, so download again after any change.

output_directory.description: Directory to save the ZIP and extract files

tools.name: get_project_file
tools.description: Read one local-run file from a project as text, without downloading and unpacking the whole ZIP. Ask get_project_status first and use a name from its files_available list — that list is derived per SRS revision, so it is the only reliable source of valid names (this tool does not carry a copy of it). env.txt is the one name that takes env_type: local is what download_project ships for running on your machine, deployment is the bucket deploy_project uses, and the web console cannot fetch the deployment one at all, which is the main reason to use this tool. Credential files in that list return a placeholder string, not a real secret — read them to see which credentials exist, never to obtain one. Use download_project when you want every file at once, and configure_environment to change environment values rather than read them.

file_name.description: File name exactly as it appears in get_project_status's files_available (for example "docker-compose.yaml" or "env.txt"). Anything else is a 404.

env_type.description: Which environment bucket to read. Only applies to "env.txt" and is ignored for other files; defaults to local. deployment returns the values deploy_project uses, which the web console cannot reach through this path.

tools.name: verify_local_run
tools.description: Get the health-check URLs for a project's locally running containers. Use it after configure_environment + download_project and after starting the containers with `docker compose up -d`, to confirm the local run is actually up — request each URL and expect a success response. A component that started correctly answers with a JSON body containing status: "ok". Returns one URL per api_server component; an empty list means this project has no HTTP-serving component, not that something failed. The paths are composed by the backend from the build's infra version, so do not guess them.

tools.name: get_messages
tools.description: Read the conversation history (human/AI turns and progress events) for a project, newest first. Use this to review what was already asked and answered during the requirements interview before calling send_message again. Unlike get_progress, this includes messages inherited from parent revisions of an updated SRS. Secrets in the stored text are already redacted by the backend.

limit.description: How many messages to fetch. Omit for the backend default.

include_progress.description: Include role=progress pipeline events (default: true). Set false to see only the human/AI interview turns.

tools.name: get_frontend_status
tools.description: Get the state of the web frontend BackendX generates for a project's backend (Beta): whether one is being generated, failed, built, or live, and at which address. After a backend build BackendX can generate the app's screens itself — as part of the pipeline when automatic generation is on, or on request with generate_frontend — and a built frontend ships inside the managed deployment (deploy_project) at its own address. state.kind summarises it: generating (poll this tool about every five seconds), ineligible (this project cannot have one — e.g. the customer builds their own app; use get_api_clipboard), stalled (the run ran out of AI tokens), failed (generate_frontend mode="retry" reuses finished stages), live (served at url — give the user that address), built (not served yet — deploy_project ships it) or none (nothing generated; generate_frontend can start one when can_generate is true). note and next_actions say what to do for the current state. url is deterministic and present even before deployment, so only live=true means it is actually being served. With include_preflight (default true) the response also carries preflight: what a new generation would build — client_mode web (a web app), mobile_web (a mobile web preview of a requested native app) or console (a backend test console for a game; not generated) — and whether it can start. Show client_mode to the user before calling generate_frontend and pass it back as accept_mode. Reading this never spends tokens, though the first preflight for a revision can take a few seconds. Read-only; requires view access to the project.

include_preflight.description: Also read the preflight verdict (what a new generation would build). Default true; pass false to skip it when only polling a run.

tools.name: generate_frontend
tools.description: Start generating the web frontend (the app's screens) BackendX builds for a finished backend (Beta). mode "new" (default) generates one for the latest revision — or for `revision` (an SRS id: pass frontend.deployed_srs_id from get_frontend_status to build for the revision that is deployed while a newer change request is still in progress); mode "retry" continues the last FAILED run, reusing the stages it finished. THIS SPENDS AI TOKENS: a run is charged when it finishes (done or partial) and a failed run costs nothing, so confirm=true is required and only after the user agreed. Before a new generation, show the user what will be built — get_frontend_status preflight.client_mode (web, or mobile_web for a requested native app) — and pass it as accept_mode: if the verdict changed by then the call is refused with CLIENT_MODE_MISMATCH instead of charging for something else. The run is asynchronous: the response returns enqueued=true at once; poll get_frontend_status about every five seconds (a run takes minutes). A built frontend ships inside the managed deployment: deploy_project (re)deploys the stack with it, at the revision it targets (get_frontend_status explains the cases where that is not what the user wants). Refusals: INSUFFICIENT_TOKENS (no AI tokens left — get_plan, purchase_tokens or get_upgrade_url), BACKEND_NOT_READY, FRONTEND_RUNNING, FRONTEND_EXISTS (one frontend per revision), CLIENT_MODE_NOT_SUPPORTED / CUSTOMER_BUILDS_OWN_APP (build your own client with get_api_clipboard), CLIENT_MODE_MISMATCH, NOTHING_TO_RETRY, REVISION_NOT_FOUND, SAMPLE_PROJECT. Requires the interview-chat capability on the project; there is no plan gate.

mode.description: "new" (default) generates a frontend for the revision; "retry" continues the last failed run, reusing its finished stages so only the remaining work is charged.

accept_mode.description: The client mode the user was shown and agreed to (get_frontend_status preflight.client_mode). Only for mode "new". When given and it no longer matches, the start is refused (CLIENT_MODE_MISMATCH) instead of charged. Only web and mobile_web are generated — a preflight of console (a game's backend test console) means no frontend can be generated, so do not ask the user to approve spending tokens on it.

revision.description: SRS id to build for (default: the latest revision). Use frontend.deployed_srs_id from get_frontend_status to match the deployed backend.

confirm.description: Must be true: the user agreed to spend AI tokens on generating (or retrying) the frontend.

tools.name: get_deploy_readiness
tools.description: Check whether a project can be deployed and, if not, exactly what is blocking it. Returns the managed-hosting pricing-consent record and the deployment questionnaire state (complete / missing / blocked). Call this first when deploy_project fails with PRICING_CONSENT_REQUIRED or QUESTIONNAIRE_INCOMPLETE, and call it EARLY on any project — some answers rule out BackendX-managed deployment for as long as they stand as the current answer, and finding that out after the pipeline has run wastes the whole build. Resolve missing answers with submit_deploy_questionnaire; a blocked entry is a different thing — its reasons split into resolvable and not, and blocked_hint in the response sorts them. Pass the same revision you intend to deploy — the gate is evaluated against that build. Read pricing_consent as history, not as a standing permission: the web console presents the pricing policy and records a FRESH consent on every deployment, so consented=true only says some earlier deployment was consented to. Present the policy and call accept_pricing_consent again for this deployment rather than treating an existing record as a reason to skip the step. The questionnaire response normally carries an MCP-derived stages map (item_id -> project_start | deploy) even when include_definition is false, plus not_presented — the items no BackendX screen asks any more (presented=false); if stages is ever absent (the backend did not serve the item definitions), treat the axis as unknown rather than assuming. It changes how missing should be read. A project_start item in missing.legal (restricted_services_ack) means this project skipped the declaration the web console collects before a project is even created — collect it with get_consent_questions and record it with submit_deploy_questionnaire. Items in not_presented never appear in missing (unanswered they pass the gate) — do not ask them; an answer already on record for one of them still counts, so a stored blocking answer there shows up in blocked. Also note build_facts.psp_modules here: it is what the payment_posture answer must be derived from, not something to ask the user about. The operator card (operator_legal_name, contacts) is filled only from answers the user confirms: questionnaire.defaults and questionnaire.suggested_answers are SUGGESTIONS that are not saved (operator_note explains), and until the card is recorded the app's privacy notice page is not published. privacy_policy_url at the top level is the address where BackendX publishes the end-user privacy notice for this app (the same before and after deployment; null when the cloud is not configured) — give it to the user to link from their app; there is nothing to paste or confirm. See get_consent_questions when you need the question wording itself — it works without a project.

revision.description: SRS revision to evaluate the gate against (see list_revisions). Omit for the latest deployable build.

lang.description: BCP-47 language for questionnaire item text (default: en). Unsupported values fall back to en.

include_definition.description: Include the full questionnaire item definitions (ids, titles, allowed option ids). Default false — they are thousands of tokens and only needed when composing answers for submit_deploy_questionnaire.

tools.name: accept_pricing_consent
tools.description: Record the account owner's consent to the BackendX managed-hosting pricing policy for a project. This writes a legally meaningful, append-only audit record and is a hard precondition for deploy_project — without it the deployment is refused with PRICING_CONSENT_REQUIRED. The consent belongs to a deployment, not to the project: the web console presents the policy and records a FRESH consent every time the user deploys, so do the same. An existing consented=true from get_deploy_readiness is a record of a past deployment, not a reason to skip this step. Before you set confirm=true you have to show the user what they are agreeing to, and this API does not serve the policy text — so these are the seven operating-policy points the web console shows (policy version 2026-10-shared), and you must put them to the user in their own language: (1) This project is billed automatically on the same day each month under its subscription plan. (2) BackendX emails a notice before each scheduled payment. (3) The plan can be changed at any time; if the subscription is cancelled, the service goes down on the next billing date. (4) [paid plans] On a paid plan, even past the included limit the service keeps running, and the overage is added to the next invoice. (5) [paid plans] On a paid plan, API calls only can be set to stop at the limit (configure_hard_stop). Database usage cannot be capped by nature, so it is always added. (6) [Sandbox] The free (Sandbox) plan has no overage charges; instead, API calls stop at the monthly limit until the next reset day, and this limit cannot be lifted. (7) [Sandbox] A free-plan deployment stays up for 60 minutes per month in total, pauses after 10 minutes without requests and wakes on the next one. If the database and file storage together exceed 1GB, new uploads are refused and the deployment may be stopped. Lead with the points that are true for THIS project's plan (get_plan: plan_code sandbox -> points 6-7, any paid plan -> points 4-5) and then mention the others, because the two sets contradict each other: on a paid plan going over the limit keeps the service running and bills the overage without an error message, while on Sandbox nothing is billed and things stop instead. Calling this tool without confirm returns exactly which points apply to the project. Do not summarise the usage points away. (Not part of the policy text, but worth saying: file downloads from the app's storage stop at the plan's monthly allowance by default — see configure_hard_stop.) Check the current state with get_deploy_readiness first.

confirm.description: Must be true. Records a binding consent on behalf of the account owner. It is an append-only audit record; withdrawal exists in the backend API (an authenticated DELETE requiring the higher MANAGE_DEPLOYMENT_LIFECYCLE capability) but is not exposed in the web console or through any MCP tool, so treat the record as standing unless the user pursues that path with BackendX support. Set it only after the human has been shown the seven policy points in this tool's description and has said yes to them.

policy_version.description: Opaque policy identifier. Defaults to the managed-shared policy version this MCP server ships with; required explicitly for any other pool.

policy_snapshot.description: Optional snapshot of the policy text/hash that was shown to the user.

tools.name: submit_deploy_questionnaire
tools.description: Record answers to the deployment questionnaire (append-only legal/audit records). Every required item must be answered and no answer may be disqualifying before deploy_project will accept a deployment. Send one item or all of them; re-answering an item supersedes the previous answer, but the superseded row stays in the audit trail forever. Use get_consent_questions for the item ids and allowed option ids (it works before a project exists), get_deploy_readiness with include_definition=true for a given project's current state, and get_deployment_data_categories for the data_categories_confirmed table. Answering watchdog_email_optin also flips the service_down ops notification (see configure_ops_notifications). Returns the updated complete/missing/blocked state, so you do not need to call get_deploy_readiness again (a stages map is attached when the public questionnaire definition is reachable; if stages is absent, use get_deploy_readiness for the stage axis). These answers are legal disclosures made on the account owner's behalf — do not guess values; ask the user. Six rules decide whether the record you write is usable. (1) Only the project_start items a screen still asks belong at project start — currently restricted_services_ack alone: record it right after create_project and before the first send_message. It must be the JSON boolean true — the server rejects 'true'/'yes'/1 by identity, and batch validation is atomic, so one bad value rejects the whole call. Do NOT ask or submit the items get_consent_questions lists under not_asked (presented=false: end_user_jurisdictions, minors_in_scope, age_gating_measures, sensitive_data_in_scope): unanswered they do not count as missing and the interview applies defaults, but a recorded answer counts — a 'yes' to minors_in_scope or sensitive_data_in_scope rules out managed deployment where a web-console user is never asked. Record one only if the user volunteers it and explicitly wants it on record — submitting one requires confirm_not_presented=true (and age_gating_measures only alongside minors_in_scope='no'). (2) payment_posture is not a question to put to the user. Read build_facts.psp_modules from get_deploy_readiness and derive it: empty list -> 'none', non-empty -> 'psp_tokens' — the same two-way rule the web console applies (it never emits 'psp_with_metadata' either; build_facts does not carry enough to justify it, so only submit 'psp_with_metadata' when the user has positively confirmed, after inspecting the generated schema via get_docs or download_source, that the build stores card metadata such as last-4 / brand / expiry — never from inference). Read the derived sentence back to the user for confirmation instead of asking an open question about payments — the web console works exactly this way and therefore can never emit raw_card, whereas an open question can, and raw_card disqualifies managed deployment for as long as it stands as the current answer, with the row kept forever in the audit trail. The server also cross-checks the answer against the build, so a guess produces a blocked item rather than progress. (3) There is no privacy-notice confirmation to submit: BackendX publishes the end-user privacy notice for the deployed app itself, at privacy_policy_url (get_deploy_readiness), built from the operator details and the data-category confirmation. Give the user that address to link from their app. privacy_block_embedded is a retired item — never submit it (the backend refuses it as retired_item). (4) Optional items: leave the key out entirely when there is no value. Sending "" is a valid answer meaning 'erase what I gave before' — it writes a new audit row and removes that field from the published privacy notice. (5) dpa_acceptance is the sharpest case: it records the human's acceptance of the Data Processing Agreement for this project. Fetch the DPA with get_legal_status (doc_key "dpa"), show the human the full text (or its read_url), and only after they accept submit {accepted: true, dpa_version: <the version you showed>} — the version of the text actually shown, never one you did not show. The DPA is accepted only here, per project; record_legal_consent refuses it. When a DPA revision that needs consent takes effect, an earlier acceptance stops counting (blocked reason dpa_reconsent_required) and the same step is repeated with the new version. (6) The operator card (operator_legal_name, service_display_name, customer_privacy_contact_email/phone, customer_breach_contact_email/phone) is recorded only from values sent here, and until it is recorded the app's privacy notice page and its sign-in consent screen are not published. get_deploy_readiness offers defaults and suggested_answers for these — they are SUGGESTIONS (earlier projects' values, the account's sign-in email), not answers: show them to the user and submit only the values the user confirms or corrects. operator_legal_name is the company or trade name (or the service name) the user gives — never fill it with the account holder's personal name. A blocked item is not an invitation to try other values: the gate follows the latest answer, so a re-answer only belongs when the earlier answer misstated the service — if the blocking answer is TRUE of the service, changing it would falsify a legal record, and the honest paths are self-hosting (download_source / download_project) or, for restricted_category (which is not a questionnaire item at all), BackendX support. Submitting a blocking option in the first place requires confirm_blocking=true.

answers.description: item_id -> value. Omit optional items entirely when they have no value — "" is not 'no value', it is an explicit erase that writes another audit row. Values are validated server-side against the item definition, which is the single source of truth; a rejected value comes back with the exact reason.

revision.description: SRS revision the srs-scoped answers belong to (see list_revisions). Omit for the latest deployable build.

confirm_blocking.description: Required only when answers contain an option that rules out managed deployment while it stands as the current answer: minors_in_scope="yes", sensitive_data_in_scope="yes" or payment_posture="raw_card". Set it to true only after the user has stated that answer themselves AND has been told in plain words what it costs — the record is append-only, so the row outlives any later correction. Never set it just to get past the error.

confirm_not_presented.description: Required only when answers contain an item no BackendX screen asks any more (presented=false — get_consent_questions lists them under not_asked). Unanswered, such an item passes the deploy gate; once recorded it counts like any other answer and stays in the append-only audit trail. Set it to true only when the user volunteered that answer and explicitly wants it on record.

tools.name: get_deployment_data_categories
tools.description: List the personal-data categories the pipeline derived from the generated schema for a build. This is the canonical list that the data_categories_confirmed questionnaire answer must match key for key — submit_deploy_questionnaire rejects a confirmation whose key set differs. Pass the same revision you intend to deploy.

revision.description: SRS revision (see list_revisions). Omit for the latest deployable build.

lang.description: BCP-47 language for the category labels (default: en). Unsupported values fall back to en.

tools.name: deploy_project
tools.description: Deploy a completed project (ReadyToRun) to the BackendX managed shared pool. Optionally target a specific SRS revision; omit to use the latest deployable. Whether a project may deploy at all is decided by its PLAN (see get_plan); there is no per-deployment charge and no account balance involved. On the free Sandbox plan there is also a monthly cap on how long a deployment may RUN, reported as sandbox_runtime by get_deployment_status — once it is used up this call is refused with UPTIME_QUOTA_EXHAUSTED until the reset date. Requires a recorded pricing consent (accept_pricing_consent) and a complete deployment questionnaire (submit_deploy_questionnaire) — check both with get_deploy_readiness before calling this. The pricing consent belongs to this deployment, not to the project: the web console presents the pricing policy and records a fresh consent every time the user deploys, so present it and call accept_pricing_consent for THIS deployment. An existing consented=true is a record of a past deployment, not a standing permission to skip the step. If BackendX generated a web frontend for this project (get_frontend_status), it is included in this deployment automatically — nothing extra to deploy — unless get_frontend_status reports include_in_compose=false (switched out of deployments). The frontend that ships is the one built for the revision being deployed. Track it afterwards: Poll get_deployment_status about every three seconds until status is "active" AND deployment_url is non-empty (url_pending false) — right after a deploy or resume turns active the backend withholds the URL (deployment_url "") until the server actually answers, for up to about five minutes, so "active" alone is not the end. Do not stop just because progress is null. Stop polling if status becomes failed, expired or removed. progress.stage walks queued -> preparing -> database -> deploying_server -> (scaling_out) -> waiting_for_server -> ready; if it stays on the same stage for more than six minutes, treat that as abnormal and report it instead of polling forever. Never read a single failed request as a failed deployment. A 503 from the deployed API later on is a different thing again and also not a failure: on the free tier a server that has gone idle is stopped, and the next request answers 503 with a Retry-After header and a body like {"reason":"waking","retry_after":<seconds>} while the stack comes back up, which is the wake-up rather than an outage — wait the number of seconds the server gave (it is an estimate, not a fixed 15, and can reach several minutes) and retry the request; when the body says "state":"scaling_out" no node is free yet and the wake takes minutes, so keep retrying for up to about ten minutes. Do not call resume_deployment or open an incident for it (get_deployment_status sandbox_runtime shows whether this is what happened). Requests to the app's own web address (the BackendX-generated frontend, when there is one) can also answer 503 with "state":"frontend_building" or "frontend_deploying": the stack is up and the frontend is still being built or shipped — wait the Retry-After seconds and retry; it is not an outage.

revision.description: SRS revision id to deploy (default: latest deployable)

tools.name: get_deployment_status
tools.description: Get the managed-shared deployment status of a project, including whether it is deployed, the deployable SRS revisions, and any active ingress endpoints (URLs). status is one of requested, pending, active, paused, failed, expired, removing or removed; active and paused are the two live states, while failed, expired and removed are terminal. Poll get_deployment_status about every three seconds until status is "active" AND deployment_url is non-empty (url_pending false) — right after a deploy or resume turns active the backend withholds the URL (deployment_url "") until the server actually answers, for up to about five minutes, so "active" alone is not the end. Do not stop just because progress is null. Stop polling if status becomes failed, expired or removed. progress.stage walks queued -> preparing -> database -> deploying_server -> (scaling_out) -> waiting_for_server -> ready; if it stays on the same stage for more than six minutes, treat that as abnormal and report it instead of polling forever. The response promotes progress and derives url_pending (active but the URL is still withheld) and deploy_in_progress (keep polling) for exactly that rule; while url_pending is true there is no api_base_url yet and short_url must not be handed out either. A pause or delete is given up to one minute to reach its target, after which the request counts as accepted-but-unconfirmed rather than failed. migration_step is another reason "active" is less conclusive than it looks: it is non-null only while a pool migration is in flight, and during that window status stays "active" while the URL can time out; that is expected, not an outage, so do not open an incident or redeploy while it is set — poll until it returns to null. For the API base URL use api_base_url in this response (deployment_url, normalized): short_url is a 302 redirect hop meant for sharing and breaks POST and PUT if used as a base. On the free tier a deployment also has a MONTHLY RUNNING-TIME BUDGET, reported as sandbox_runtime: how many minutes the plan allows, how much is left right now, when it refills, why the server is paused if it is, and whether it wakes by itself. The refill time, resets_at, is this project's own monthly reset — its creation day, or its billing day once it has subscribed (kept after cancelling back to Sandbox) — and carries a time of day, so quote the value and never derive a reset date from the calendar; a Sandbox project's blocked API calls come back at that same reset, give or take a couple of minutes while enforcement refreshes. Read sandbox_runtime_note before acting on a paused deployment, because the three pause reasons need three different responses. "idle" with automatic wake-up means DO NOTHING: the server restarts on the next request, so calling resume_deployment is pointless — and that first request answers 503 with a Retry-After header while the stack comes up, which is the wake-up rather than an outage, so wait and retry it instead of reporting a failure or opening an incident. "quota_exhausted", or zero seconds remaining, means both resume_deployment and deploy_project are refused until the refill date, and only waiting or upgrading clears it. "manual" means the server was stopped deliberately and resume_deployment is the way back; note that after resets_at has passed a previously exhausted pause is reported as "manual" precisely because it has become restartable again. sandbox_runtime is null on a paid plan and absent entirely when the project has never been deployed, and reading this tool never consumes any of the budget. Requests to the app's own web address (the BackendX-generated frontend, when there is one) can also answer 503 with "state":"frontend_building" or "frontend_deploying": the stack is up and the frontend is still being built or shipped — wait the Retry-After seconds and retry; it is not an outage.

tools.name: pause_deployment
tools.description: Pause a managed-shared deployment: the docker stack is taken down while the domain, database, secrets and compose workdir are all kept. Your API stops serving traffic until you call resume_deployment, so confirm with the user before calling this. Subscription billing is unaffected. The call only accepts the request — the backend flips the status to "paused" once the stack is actually down, so poll get_deployment_status for status="paused" instead of assuming success. Poll about every three seconds and allow up to a minute; if it has not flipped by then the request is accepted-but-unconfirmed rather than failed, so re-check before retrying.

tools.name: resume_deployment
tools.description: Bring a paused managed-shared deployment back up (the counterpart of pause_deployment). The preserved compose workdir is redeployed, so the domain, database and secrets are unchanged and there is no extra charge. CHECK WHY IT IS PAUSED FIRST with get_deployment_status: when sandbox_runtime.stop_reason is "idle" and auto_resume_enabled is true, the server comes back on its own as soon as a request arrives and calling this is unnecessary; when it is "quota_exhausted", or remaining_seconds is 0, this call is refused with UPTIME_QUOTA_EXHAUSTED until the monthly free uptime refills at resets_at, and only "manual" is the plain case this tool is for. The call only accepts the request — status normally reaches "active" within about a minute (past that the request is accepted-but-unconfirmed rather than failed), but the backend withholds deployment_url until the server answers, so a resume is done only when the URL is back: Poll get_deployment_status about every three seconds until status is "active" AND deployment_url is non-empty (url_pending false) — right after a deploy or resume turns active the backend withholds the URL (deployment_url "") until the server actually answers, for up to about five minutes, so "active" alone is not the end. Do not stop just because progress is null. Stop polling if status becomes failed, expired or removed. progress.stage walks queued -> preparing -> database -> deploying_server -> (scaling_out) -> waiting_for_server -> ready; if it stays on the same stage for more than six minutes, treat that as abnormal and report it instead of polling forever. A first failed request is not a failed resume.

tools.name: stop_deployment
tools.description: Delete the managed-shared deployment of a project. The deployed database is destroyed permanently and there is no recovery — redeploying later starts from an empty database. The source, SRS revisions and docker artifacts are kept, so the project can be deployed again at no extra cost; deployment is included in the plan. Subscription billing is NOT cancelled by this — that is cancel_subscription, a separate decision. A project with a live deployment cannot be deleted, so if the goal is deleting the project this comes first: stop the deployment, then call get_deletion_preview again. Because this cannot be undone you must pass confirm=true. If you only want to take the API offline temporarily, use pause_deployment instead — it keeps the domain, data and secrets.

confirm.description: Must be true to confirm. The deployed database is permanently destroyed and cannot be recovered.

tools.name: get_ops_summary
tools.description: Get the operations summary for a deployed project: server health status and KPI counts over a time range. Requires the project to be deployed (see deploy_project). The two halves of the response have very different standing. The KPI counts are real, read from the incident table. server_status is NOT: no health source is wired up yet, so the backend returns a hardcoded "healthy" for every project — never report it as evidence that the service is up, and use list_incidents and get_ops_usage for that instead. The other values the schema advertises (overloaded, stopped, errorAutoRecovery, errorExternalService) are not currently emitted at all.

range.description: How far back the KPI counts cover (default: 24h). These are the only accepted windows — there is no 7d or 30d.

tools.name: list_incidents
tools.description: List operational incidents for a deployed project. category is a required selector, not an optional filter — one call returns one category. The three categories are a division of labour by WHO HAS TO ACT, not by status class and not a progress bar: needsAttention are issues BackendX cannot fix itself, so a human has to act on them; inProgress are ones BackendX has taken up and is working on; resolved are closed. Do not read 5xx as "BackendX fixes it" and 4xx as "the user fixes it" — once the automatic triage verdict lands, a 4xx that is the generated code's fault (missing_endpoint, code_is_wrong) moves to inProgress, and a 5xx BackendX cannot fix (customer_config, missing_seed_data, external_dependency) moves to needsAttention; incidents the user already moved are left where they are. So a long needsAttention list is work for the user, not something that clears itself. Requires the project to be deployed. Use get_incident for one incident's timeline and update_incident_status to move it along. List items carry no triage verdict or AI-prompt eligibility — those are only on the detail from get_incident.

range.description: How far back to look (default: 24h). These are the only accepted windows — there is no 7d or 30d.

category.description: Which category to list. Required — the backend rejects a call without it. needsAttention: the user has to act. inProgress: BackendX is working on it. resolved: closed.

page_size.description: Number of incidents per page (1-100, default 10)

tools.name: get_ops_usage
tools.description: Get usage metrics for a deployed project against the plan quota: API calls, storage (database plus the app's cloud-storage files, one quota) and — when the app stores files — file downloads, plus per-day request counts. Requires the project to be deployed. API calls: the block decision is window_calls >= total_calls — window_calls counts calls since window_start with the same counter the enforcer uses, and resets_at is when the window rolls over (quote it as given, never compute a calendar date). percent and used_calls are a display figure over the last (up to) 30 days, NOT the blocking test. window_calls null means the metrics could not be read, in which case nothing is blocked. total_calls is the quota the enforcer applies — on Sandbox its catalog quota even without a subscription — and null only on plans with no numeric API-call quota (Builder, Enterprise); never read null as unlimited on a Sandbox project, and do not judge an overage while it is null. Calls the app makes to BackendX services on its behalf (its cloud storage) count as project API calls too. What crossing a quota does depends on the plan. On a PAID plan it does NOT stop the service — the excess is billed on the next invoice, so usage above the limit is a cost signal rather than an error (unless configure_hard_stop has turned on the API-call hard stop, which rejects calls instead); a subscription whose payment failed and is being retried (past due) keeps its paid plan's limits. On the free Sandbox plan nothing is ever billed: API calls over the quota are ALWAYS blocked until resets_at, and db.hard=true means the deployment stops once the storage limit is exceeded. db: the storage gauge (database + cloud-storage files), omitted only when the plan has no numeric quota (Builder, Enterprise); db.used_bytes = 0 means "not measured yet" — measurement is a roughly five-minute beat and stays 0 before deployment — NOT an empty database. transfer: file downloads from the app's cloud storage in the current window, present only when the app stores files; transfer.hard=true (the default, always on Sandbox) means downloads stop at the allowance, false means the excess bills per started GB (configure_hard_stop transfer_hard_stop; the list price is get_plan's indicative_unit_prices.transfer_overage on a USD subscription). The backend never fabricates these figures because they sit next to billing, so do not fill them in either. The most recent day in the per-day series is still aggregating and will keep rising, so do not compare it with a completed day. The response carries no forecast — the backend deliberately never predicts a limit-reach date.
