Use configure_hard_stop to choose blocking over billing on a paid plan, get_usage_by_date to drill into one day, and get_plan to see what is already accruing (its overage_note states this plan's rule).

tools.name: configure_hard_stop
tools.description: View or change a project's two hard stops: api_hard_stop (API calls above the monthly quota) and transfer_hard_stop (file downloads from the app's BackendX cloud storage above the plan's monthly download allowance — limits.transfer_gb in get_plan_catalog). Omit both to read the current values, and report what the backend returns rather than inferring it from the plan; locked and locked_reason say whether they can be changed at all — judge that from locked, never from the plan code. Locks: locked_reason "sandbox" is the free Sandbox plan, where BOTH stops are ALWAYS ON and cannot be turned off — Sandbox has no billing period to charge overage to, so API calls above the monthly quota are refused until the project's next monthly reset (while deployed, get_deployment_status reports it as sandbox_runtime.resets_at) and downloads stop at the allowance; writing true is accepted as a no-op and writing false is refused with SANDBOX_HARD_STOP_REQUIRED, which means the setting stays on, not that something broke — do not retry it; only the reset or upgrading to a paid plan that includes hosting (get_upgrade_url) lifts a Sandbox block. locked_reason "past_due" means a subscription payment failed and Stripe is retrying it: the values already set keep applying, but any change is refused with NO_ACTIVE_SUBSCRIPTION until the payment settles — the fix is updating the card in the billing portal (get_billing_portal_url), not a new checkout. On an unlocked PAID plan BOTH settings carry a risk, so confirm the intent with the user before changing either. api_hard_stop false (the default) means calls above the monthly quota keep being served and the excess is billed on the next invoice — spend accrues silently with no error; true means the deployed service starts REJECTING API traffic the moment the quota is exhausted, which is an outage for its callers. transfer_hard_stop is the other way round by default: true (the default) refuses download links once the allowance is used up, false keeps serving them and bills the excess per started GB (no BackendX API serves that price; quote get_plan's indicative_unit_prices.transfer_overage as an estimate, which is present only when the subscription bills in USD). Neither caps database storage: DB overage cannot be blocked at all on a paid plan (writes are never refused for quota reasons — data integrity), so DB excess always bills and its usage percent can run past 100. Do not tell the user that turning these on caps their overage spend outright. Changing them requires billing permission (owner only). In the response, changed only says whether a write was sent; the values are what the backend now holds. See get_ops_usage for how much of each quota is used and get_plan for the plan.

api_hard_stop.description: New API-call hard stop. Omit to leave it unchanged (omit both settings to only read). On Sandbox only true is accepted (a no-op).

transfer_hard_stop.description: New file-download hard stop for the app's cloud storage (default true = stop at the monthly download allowance; false = keep serving and bill the excess per started GB). Omit to leave it unchanged. On Sandbox only true is accepted (a no-op).

tools.name: configure_ops_notifications
tools.description: View or change which operational events email the project owner. Omit settings to read the current values. Any subset of keys may be sent; omitted keys keep their stored value, and the response always contains every key. email_enabled is the master switch. service_down is also written by the watchdog_email_optin questionnaire answer (see submit_deploy_questionnaire) — the backend keeps the two in sync. The server_* keys cover new and resolved 5xx incidents and the client_* keys new and repeating 4xx incidents — a split by status class, not by who has to act: an incident's category follows ownership (see list_incidents), so a 5xx can need the user (customer_config, missing_seed_data, external_dependency) and a 4xx can be BackendX's to fix. client_new is off by default, because a 4xx is already visible to the client that made the call in its own response and the email is mostly noise. Whether an email is actually sent is decided server-side; these are only preferences, and mute_incident_notifications can suppress a single noisy incident without changing any of them.

settings.description: Keys to change. Omit entirely to read the current settings without changing them.

email_enabled.description: Master switch for all operational emails.

usage_limit_enabled.description: Email when API usage crosses a quota threshold.

usage_limit_thresholds.description: Which quota percentages trigger a usage email. Any subset of [50, 80, 90]; an empty array disables the thresholds.

service_down.description: Email when the watchdog sees the whole service down.

service_recovered.description: Email when the service comes back up.

server_resolved.description: Email when a 5xx incident is resolved.

tools.name: configure_autofix_redeploy
tools.description: View or change whether BackendX's automatic repairs are DEPLOYED automatically. When triage finds a defect in the generated backend (or in the frontend BackendX generated), BackendX builds a repaired revision by itself — that happens either way and costs nothing. This switch only decides what happens next: ON means the repaired revision replaces the running deployment in place as soon as it is built, WITHOUT anyone reviewing it first (no charge); OFF (the default) means it waits as fix.state "ready" in get_incident and the owner gets a "fix ready" email, and someone deploys it with deploy_project. Omit redeploy_enabled to read the current value. Turning it on affects the next repair onwards; a fix already waiting in "ready" still needs deploy_project. Ask the user before turning it on — it lets code changes reach their live service unattended. Reading needs view access to the deployment dashboard; changing needs the deployment-lifecycle capability. See get_incident (fix.auto_redeploy) for where this shows up.

redeploy_enabled.description: true = deploy BackendX's repaired revisions automatically as soon as they are built; false = leave them waiting for deploy_project. Omit to read the current value.

tools.name: rename_project
tools.description: Change a project's label (title).

tools.name: get_deletion_preview
tools.description: Read-only check of whether a project can be deleted, what blocks it, and what deleting it will charge. Call this BEFORE delete_project: its revision is that tool's required preview_revision, and its charge is the amount billed the moment the deletion goes through — amounts are Stripe minor units with a currency, and charge_total_display spells the total out. next_actions tells you what to do: stop_deployment when a live deployment blocks deletion (then preview again); nothing when a non-deployment blocker such as a sample project stands (an admin has to lift it); delete_project when can_delete is true, after showing the user the charge if it is above zero. It also reports subscription_notice when the project still has a running paid subscription: deleting cancels it immediately with no refund for the remaining paid time, which is why the web console routes people to cancel first and delete later. Relay that before the user decides. Owner only. The revision expires after about 15 minutes and is invalidated by any change to billing state, so fetch it right before deleting rather than holding it. Deleting a subscribed project cancels its subscription immediately; to keep the project but stop paying, use cancel_subscription instead.

tools.name: delete_project
tools.description: Delete a project. Treat it as permanent: nothing in this API brings it back, and the project disappears from list_projects at once along with every member's access. There is one narrow escape hatch worth telling the user about if they deleted the wrong project — the backend soft-deletes, keeping the owner link, member rows, invitations and message keys for about 30 days before a sweep severs them for good, so BackendX SUPPORT can still restore it by hand within that window. That is a support request, not something any tool here can do, and it expires. It is a two-step operation: call get_deletion_preview first and pass its revision as preview_revision — that is how the server confirms the state the user was shown (blockers and charge) is still current, and the revision expires after about 15 minutes. Deleting a subscribed project has IMMEDIATE FINANCIAL EFFECTS: the subscription is cancelled on the spot (not at period end — that is cancel_subscription, a separate decision) and any unbilled items in the preview's charge (an open invoice, or unbilled overage from the current window) are charged to the card right now. If charge.amount_total in the preview is above zero, show the user that amount and get their agreement before setting confirm=true. If the project still has a running paid subscription, deleting now throws away the remaining paid time — there is no refund — so get_deletion_preview reports subscription_notice and this tool repeats it on the confirmation gate; the gentler route is cancel_subscription and then deleting after the period ends. A project with a live deployment cannot be deleted — stop_deployment first, then preview again. There is no partial success: if the settlement charge fails, the project and its subscription are left exactly as they were. Owner only. Retrying after a network failure is safe with the same preview_revision (the request is idempotent per revision); after PAYMENT_FAILED or PREVIEW_STALE fetch a fresh preview.

preview_revision.description: The revision from a fresh get_deletion_preview call for this project. Required — it is how the server confirms nothing changed since the user saw the cost. Expires in about 15 minutes.

confirm.description: Must be true to confirm deletion. No tool can undo it — only a support request within roughly 30 days can — and on a subscribed project it cancels the subscription and charges the preview's amount immediately.

tools.name: list_revisions
tools.description: List the SRS revision summaries of a project (change subject and bullets per revision). Useful to see how requirements evolved and which revisions are available to deploy.

tools.name: upload_attachment
tools.description: Attach a local file to a project as requirements context. The file is processed asynchronously on the server (summary extraction → reflected into the SRS). Returns a task_id. Only PDF, PPTX, PNG and JPEG files are accepted, and the content type is taken from the file extension — a legacy .ppt is rejected, so convert it to .pptx first. Each file must stay under the backend's per-file size cap (deployment-configurable) and the project has a cumulative attachment quota on top of the plan's file-upload allowance. The project must not be busy with another task; retry shortly if it is. Security: the file at file_path is read and uploaded to the backend as-is — only attach files the user intends to share, never credentials/keys or other sensitive files.

file_path.description: Absolute path to the local file to attach. Its extension decides the content type sent to the backend, so it must be .pdf, .pptx, .png, .jpg or .jpeg. Its bytes are uploaded to the backend — do not pass sensitive files.

langcode.description: Language code for processing the attachment

tools.name: download_attachment
tools.description: Download a file that was attached to this project as requirements context, saving it to disk. This is the counterpart of upload_attachment, which returns only a task_id and never an attachment id. To find an id, call get_messages and look at the messages with the attachment role: their content is JSON shaped {"attachments": [{"id": ..., "file_name": ..., "content_type": ...}]}, and the id there is what this tool takes. Attachments are PDF, PPTX, PNG or JPEG, so they are written to a file rather than returned inline. They are swept after a retention window and cannot be recovered once that happens.

attachment_id.description: Attachment id, taken from the "attachments" JSON inside an attachment-role message returned by get_messages.

output_directory.description: Directory to save the attachment file into

tools.name: get_api_clipboard
tools.description: Get everything needed to build a frontend, web page, mobile app or any other client against this backend, packaged as one ready-to-paste prompt. CALL THIS FIRST whenever the user wants to build a UI or client app on top of a project built here — it is the tool behind the web console's "Copy AI prompt" button. The system_prompt it returns is a complete instruction set ("integrate a client against this backend") with the full API reference embedded, and it carries the live deployment's base URL automatically when the project has one, so the generated client targets the real host instead of a placeholder: hand it to whatever agent or tool writes the client, rather than re-deriving the endpoints yourself. Prefer it over get_docs(doc="api") for this purpose — that one returns the bare endpoint reference with no integration instructions. The response also carries api_doc (every component merged into one Markdown document, OpenAPI included) and markdown_apis / openapi_apis (component name -> document) if the documentation on its own is what you need. Access is granted by the project's plan rather than bought per project, and every current plan includes it, so a refusal here almost always means the pipeline has not produced the API documentation yet — wait_for_pipeline, then retry. Set audience to match who the client is for: "frontend" removes the admin-only endpoints from the documentation so a customer-facing app cannot call them, "admin" keeps everything and lists the administrative routes with their required roles at the top, and omitting it gives the older combined document. Be ready for a big result: the document is embedded in system_prompt and repeated as api_doc and as the per-component maps, which came to roughly 140 KB even for a small project. When that is too large to work with, ASK THE USER whether to switch to link=true — never turn it on by yourself, because it publishes the API documentation at an unauthenticated URL.

integration_prompt.description: Prepend an instruction to build a client against this backend (default true). Set false ONLY when you want the API documentation on its own — the response then has no system_prompt, and a coding tool handed the bare document is left to guess what to do with it.

include_deployed_base_url.description: Embed the live deployment's base URL in the prompt so the generated client points at it. Defaults to TRUE here (the raw API defaults to false) — a deployed project should never hand out a prompt aimed at a placeholder host, and asking for it on an undeployed project costs nothing but an empty deployed_base_urls. Pass false only to deliberately leave the live URL out.

link.description: Deliver the documentation as a public share link instead of inlining it: the response drops api_doc / markdown_apis / openapi_apis and returns api_doc_url, and the prompt tells the client to fetch that URL. It shrinks a ~140 KB response to a few KB. ASK THE USER BEFORE SETTING THIS — the URL is UNAUTHENTICATED, so anyone who holds it can read this project's full API documentation, and minting it requires the share_artifacts capability. Useful when the prompt goes to a tool that can fetch URLs; useless for one that cannot. Combines with audience="frontend": the link then serves the frontend-safe document (admin endpoints removed) — the natural choice when the prompt is for building a customer-facing client.

audience.description: Who the generated client is for, which decides what the documentation contains. "frontend" strips the admin-only endpoints from both the Markdown and the OpenAPI spec and frames the prompt for an end-user app — use it when building the customer-facing client, so the generated code cannot call administrative routes. "admin" keeps the full document and puts a list of the admin endpoints, each with the role it needs, at the top of the prompt — use it when building an internal dashboard. Omit it for the historical combined prompt, which is neither stripped nor annotated.

tools.name: register_signin_redirect_uri
tools.description: Register a callback URL for the project's Sign in with BackendX (the page your frontend uses to finish sign-in). Call it as soon as a deployed frontend URL is known — production, preview domains, a native app scheme. There is no dashboard screen for this. Idempotent; at most 10 per project. Local development (http://localhost…) needs no registration. Side effect: registering also opts the deployment into the BackendX-provided sign-in settings (the oauth_backendx environment group), so configure_environment then lists those keys as provided_by_backendx — leave them alone unless you mean to replace BackendX's values for the whole group. Requires deploy permission.

uri.description: The exact callback URL BackendX sends the user back to after sign-in (https://…, or a native app scheme such as com.example.app:/oauth). Exact match — no wildcards, no fragment, no user name/password. http://localhost, 127.0.0.1 and [::1] (any port) work without registering.

tools.name: list_signin_redirect_uris
tools.description: List the callback URLs registered for the project's Sign in with BackendX, with the issuer and client ID the frontend uses.

tools.name: remove_signin_redirect_uri
tools.description: Remove a registered Sign in with BackendX callback URL (e.g. a retired preview domain). Sign-in to that URL stops working immediately.

uri.description: The registered URL, exactly as listed

tools.name: get_admin_setup_code
tools.description: Get the one-time setup code that makes the app's FIRST admin. The operator signs in to their own app as usual, opens the admin dashboard's 'become the first admin' screen and enters this code (the app's POST /_bx/admin/claim). No user ID or email is needed. It works only while the app has no admin; further admins are granted inside the dashboard. When BackendX generated the app's web frontend, setup_url is the address of that first-admin screen in it — hand the user that link together with the code. Share it only with the person who should become admin.

tools.name: get_progress
tools.description: Get the step-by-step pipeline progress messages for a project (paginated, newest first). Use this to follow detailed stage-by-stage progress; get_project_status only returns the latest few events. The response also carries failure_kind and budget, because the log alone cannot tell you why it stops: when a project runs out of AI tokens the pipeline simply goes quiet, leaving a normal-looking last entry that is easy to misread as the stage that failed. failure_kind="budget_exceeded" means exactly that, and budget_note says what clears it — resume_pipeline after the budget is raised when budget.phase is "pipeline", or re-sending the message with send_message when it is "interview". Never call retry_pipeline for a budget stop. While the requirements interview is running, interview_core_questions_remaining says how many core questions the user has not answered yet (0 = the closing confirmation; null outside the interview or when the project record could not be read).

limit.description: Number of progress items to fetch (max 100)

tools.name: download_source
tools.description: Download the generated project source code as a ZIP archive and optionally extract it. Access is granted by the project's plan, not bought per project, and starts at the Builder plan. THE ARCHIVE CONTAINS REAL SECRETS: alongside the code it ships an env.txt filled from the project's secrets store and a <database>_password.txt per database, so treat the extracted directory as credential material — do not commit it, paste it into a chat, or write it into logs. type picks which bucket fills env.txt: local (the default) for running on your machine, deployment for the values the managed deployment uses. The ZIP holds the latest revision AS OF THIS DOWNLOAD — it is a snapshot, so a later requirement change or pipeline re-run does not update the extracted files and you have to download again after any change. This differs from download_project, which only fetches local-run config files (docker-compose, etc.).

output_directory.description: Directory to save the ZIP and extract files

type.description: Which environment bucket fills the bundled env.txt: "local" (default) for running on this machine, "deployment" for the values the managed deployment runs with. It changes only that file, not the code. The two buckets are separate stores — see configure_environment.

tools.name: get_incident
tools.description: Get the details of a single operational incident (timeline, endpoint spec, etc.) for a deployed project. Use list_incidents first to find the incident id. Three fields tell you what to do next. ai_prompt_available says whether get_incident_ai_prompt will hand you a resolution prompt for this incident — a fix-the-client prompt for a 4xx that triage attributed to the caller, or an owner-facing prompt for a 5xx triaged as customer_config, missing_seed_data or external_dependency — so do not call it when this is false. triage_verdict is the platform's classification: customer_error, expected_behavior, external_dependency or inconclusive point at the caller or outside, customer_config and missing_seed_data at the project's own settings or data, missing_endpoint and code_is_wrong are defects in the generated backend, and frontend_is_wrong means the bad request came from the web frontend BackendX generated and deployed — BackendX fixes that frontend; null means triage has not run yet (it runs about every five minutes), so check again shortly. triage_caller says who sent the sampled request: shipped_frontend (the BackendX-deployed frontend) or external (any other client); null without a sample. fix is present only for a backend defect or a frontend_is_wrong incident and tracks BackendX's own automatic repair: queued or in_progress means wait; waiting (frontend defects only) means automatic frontend generation is off, so the next frontend update repairs it — generate_frontend starts one; ready with auto_redeploy=false means a repaired revision (srs_id; for a frontend defect, the repair run frontend_run_id) is built and waiting for YOU to run deploy_project; deployed means the fix is live and the incident can be moved to resolved with update_incident_status; failed means the retry budget is spent and a human has to look. auto_redeploy is the project's switch for deploying repairs unattended — configure_autofix_redeploy views or changes it (it is free; ask the user before turning it on). muted tells you whether notifications for this incident are suppressed (see mute_incident_notifications). traceback is the Python stack trace captured when the deployed app failed (null when there is none — most handled 4xx — or the sample aged out): use it to explain to the user where and why the request failed. Frames under app/managed_services/, app/byo_services/ or other platform-shipped files, or a backend-defect triage_verdict, mean the fault is in BackendX-provided code — tell the user BackendX owns that fix and do not try to patch or work around it in their code; frames in their own routes/models point at the generated app logic. Sensitive request data and every sensitive value in the traceback (database values, SQL parameters, passwords, API keys, tokens, email addresses) are masked by the backend as ***. payload_redacted=true means YOUR role cannot see error payloads (the view_error_payloads capability — owner, admin and operator by default): request.body, request.message and traceback are then left empty and ai_prompt_available is false. That is withheld, not absent — do not tell the user the request had no body or that there is no stack trace; someone with that capability can read them (get_role_matrix shows which role carries it).

tools.name: get_incident_ai_prompt
tools.description: Get a ready-to-use prompt for resolving an incident the project owner can fix. Two kinds, chosen by the backend: for a 4xx attributed to the caller, a prompt for fixing the CLIENT that calls this backend (from the decrypted sample request and response, the matching operation in the deployed API documentation, the live base URL and the triage verdict); for a 5xx that triage found fixable OUTSIDE the code — customer_config (a missing or rejected provider key, an exhausted quota), missing_seed_data (reference rows the code expects but nobody seeded) or external_dependency (a provider outage) — an owner-facing prompt with the redacted service log and stack trace and the steps: set the value in the deployment environment and redeploy, seed the data, or handle the provider. Both are assembled deterministically (no LLM) from material you cannot reconstruct yourself, so act on the prompt directly. Read ai_prompt_available in get_incident first: an untriaged incident, one triaged as a platform defect, or any other 5xx is refused here. A refusal is not a dead end — TRIAGE_PENDING clears after the next triage pass (about five minutes), and PLATFORM_WILL_FIX means BackendX is repairing the generated backend (backend_defect) or the web frontend it generated and deployed (frontend_defect) itself, so read the fix block in get_incident instead — configure_autofix_redeploy decides whether such repairs deploy themselves. The response can be large. The context flags say how much real material went in: when sample_available or doc_operation_matched is false the prompt falls back to generic guidance, and the response lists those gaps under caveats. No plan gating. Because the prompt carries the decrypted request and stack trace, it needs the view_error_payloads capability on top of the deployment-dashboard view that get_incident needs (owner, admin and operator have it by default): without it the call is refused with INSUFFICIENT_ROLE naming that capability, and get_incident shows payload_redacted=true with ai_prompt_available=false.

tools.name: update_incident_status
tools.description: Move an incident to a new status. Only three transitions exist and they all go forward: needsAttention → inProgress, needsAttention → resolved, and inProgress → resolved. NOTHING GOES BACK — "resolved" is a terminal state with no API to reopen it, and an incident cannot return from inProgress to needsAttention, so resolve only what is actually settled. Use list_incidents to see an incident's current category before transitioning it, since the allowed move depends on where it is now.

category.description: Where to move it. inProgress: start handling (only from needsAttention). resolved: close it (from either) — this cannot be undone.

tools.name: list_privacy_requests
tools.description: List the privacy requests forwarded by this project's deployed app, newest first — number, type, status, received / due time and whether it is overdue, but no content (open one with get_privacy_request). These are data-subject rights requests your deployed app's users sent through its privacy form (restriction, objection, consent withdrawal, review of an automated decision, other) — account deletion and data export are the app's own endpoints and never appear here. A response is due 10 days after receipt (Korean Personal Information Protection Act — the strictest of PIPA, GDPR's one month and CCPA's 45 days); overdue ones are flagged. Requires the handle_privacy_requests capability (the owner always has it). Filter with status, or overdue=true for open ones past their deadline — check those first.

status.description: Only this status. received / in_progress / extended are open; done / rejected are closed.

overdue.description: true: only open ones past their deadline.

tools.name: get_privacy_request
tools.description: Open one privacy request: its decrypted details, the decision note so far and the status history. requester_ref is the requester's user id in your app's own users table — look the person up there, BackendX does not know who they are. content_purged=true means the content was destroyed under the retention rule (1 year after closing); the record itself stays 3 years. Requires the handle_privacy_requests capability. This contains end users' personal data. Tell the operator only what they need to decide — summarize, do not paste the details or any contact data into other tools, files, tickets or messages.

tools.name: update_privacy_request
tools.description: Record what was done with a privacy request. status: in_progress (being handled), extended (needs longer — note with the reason AND a later due_at, at most 90 days after receipt), done or rejected (both close it and CANNOT be undone). done = the request was carried out; rejected = declined (the note is the reason the requester sees in the app). rejected and extended require note. The note is shown to the requester, so write it for them, in their language, without other people's data. A response is due 10 days after receipt (Korean Personal Information Protection Act — the strictest of PIPA, GDPR's one month and CCPA's 45 days); overdue ones are flagged. Requires the handle_privacy_requests capability. Confirm the decision with the operator before calling — you are acting for the app's operator, who is legally responsible for the answer.

status.description: New status. done / rejected are final.

note.description: Reason shown to the requester. Required for rejected and extended.

due_at.description: ISO-8601 new deadline — only with extended; later than the current one, within 90 days of receipt.

tools.name: list_abuse_reports
tools.description: List the content reports forwarded by this project's deployed app, newest first — number, type, status, received / due time and whether it is overdue, but no content (open one with get_abuse_report). These are reports your deployed app's users (signed in or anonymous) filed against content in the app — target_type / target_id name the reported item in your app's own terms. A csam report has also been passed to BackendX, which handles it as the law requires; still act on the content in your app. A response is due 10 days after receipt (Korean Personal Information Protection Act — the strictest of PIPA, GDPR's one month and CCPA's 45 days); overdue ones are flagged. Requires the handle_abuse_reports capability (the owner always has it). Filter with status, or overdue=true for open ones past their deadline — check those first.

status.description: Only this status. received / in_progress / extended are open; done / rejected are closed.

overdue.description: true: only open ones past their deadline.

tools.name: get_abuse_report
tools.description: Open one content report: its decrypted details, the decision note so far and the status history. The reporter's name and email appear only when your role carries view_reporter_contact (has_contact says whether they left any); an anonymous reporter who left an email is mailed the outcome by BackendX automatically — you do not need to contact them. content_purged=true means the content was destroyed under the retention rule (1 year after closing); the record itself stays 3 years. Requires the handle_abuse_reports capability. This contains end users' personal data. Tell the operator only what they need to decide — summarize, do not paste the details or any contact data into other tools, files, tickets or messages.

tools.name: update_abuse_report
tools.description: Record what was done with a content report. status: in_progress (being handled), extended (needs longer — note with the reason AND a later due_at, at most 90 days after receipt), done or rejected (both close it and CANNOT be undone). done = action taken on the content; rejected = report dismissed (the note is the reason the reporter is told). rejected and extended require note. The note is shown to the requester, so write it for them, in their language, without other people's data. A response is due 10 days after receipt (Korean Personal Information Protection Act — the strictest of PIPA, GDPR's one month and CCPA's 45 days); overdue ones are flagged. Requires the handle_abuse_reports capability. Confirm the decision with the operator before calling — you are acting for the app's operator, who is legally responsible for the answer.

status.description: New status. done / rejected are final.

note.description: Reason shown to the requester. Required for rejected and extended.

due_at.description: ISO-8601 new deadline — only with extended; later than the current one, within 90 days of receipt.

tools.name: get_usage_by_date
tools.description: Get the per-day API call analysis for a deployed project on a specific date: total calls, limit contribution, and top APIs. Drill-down from get_ops_usage. A day's figure is final only once the day has closed — each past day is a completed 24-hour total, but today's row is still aggregating and will keep rising. Never compare today against a completed day or read a trend from it, or you will systematically under-report current usage. monthly_total_calls can be null — no numeric quota on Builder or Enterprise, or a Sandbox project whose quota is not reported here (Sandbox is still blocked at its catalog quota — get_plan_catalog) — and limit_contribution_percent then reads 0, which means unknown, not 'no impact on the limit'.

date.description: Date in YYYY-MM-DD format. Today's figure is a partial, still-growing total.

tools.name: get_ops_resources
tools.description: Get container resource usage for a deployed project: cpu_cores, memory_bytes, net_rx_bps and net_tx_bps, averaged over window_seconds (300 by default). There is no disk metric — per-container disk IO is not available on cgroup-v2 hosts, so network throughput takes its place. Every figure is an ABSOLUTE value summed across all of the project's containers (api server, app server, database, cache), not a percentage: a project can span several shared nodes, so there is no capacity to take a percentage of. Despite the name, net_rx_bps and net_tx_bps are BYTES per second, not bits. A null means the metric was not collected — the backend never substitutes a zero, so treat null as unknown rather than idle. These are rates over the window, not instantaneous readings.

tools.name: mute_incident_notifications
tools.description: Silence email notifications for ONE incident, or unmute it again with muted=false. A muted incident is skipped even when the project's notification toggles are on, which makes this the tool for a single repeatedly-firing issue — use configure_ops_notifications instead to change what the project alerts on as a whole. Muting hides the noise, not the problem: the incident stays open and still needs resolving (see update_incident_status). The setting is stored permanently with no expiry and can be toggled back at any time, so it is reversible but nothing will remind anyone it is on — get_incident reports the current state in its muted field. Requires deployment lifecycle permission, which is more than the read-only ops tools need.

muted.description: true silences notifications for this incident; false turns them back on.

tools.name: get_github_account
tools.description: Get the GitHub account currently linked to this BackendX user (used to add you as a collaborator on generated source repos). Returns linked:false only when nothing is linked at all. The presence of user_id is what says an account is linked: if BackendX cannot reach GitHub at that moment it still reports the link with login, name and avatar_url as null, which is a degraded read and NOT a broken link — do not offer to run link_github in that case, because re-linking solves nothing and the details come back on their own.

tools.name: link_github
tools.description: Link a GitHub account using a GitHub personal access token (PAT). This is the agent-compatible alternative to the browser OAuth flow, and is required so BackendX can add you as a collaborator on generated source repositories. Linking alone opens no repository: join each project's repository with manage_repo_access(action:"join"). Create a PAT at github.com/settings/tokens.

access_token.description: GitHub personal access token (PAT) with repo access. Create one at github.com/settings/tokens.

tools.name: unlink_github
tools.description: Disconnect the GitHub account linked to this BackendX user. This is destructive and takes effect immediately: BackendX removes you from EVERY source mirror repository you take part in — not only your own projects' but also those of projects you are a member of — and withdraws any pending invitation, so you lose the ability to clone or pull them. Nothing is deleted on the BackendX side and the mirrors themselves stay. Access does NOT come back by relinking alone: link a GitHub account again with link_github (a new personal access token), then rejoin each project's repository yourself with manage_repo_access(action:"join") and accept the new GitHub invitation. Requires confirm=true. Call get_github_account first if you need to know which account is currently linked.

confirm.description: Must be true to proceed. Unlinking immediately removes you from every source repository you take part in, other members' projects included.

github_user_id.description: Optional: the user_id reported by an earlier get_github_account call. Normally omit it — the tool looks the id up itself. Pass it only when that lookup fails (GITHUB_LOOKUP_FAILED), since the backend's lookup depends on the GitHub API resolving the linked user while the unlink itself does not.

tools.name: manage_repo_access
tools.description: See, join or leave a project's GitHub source repository — for YOU, the calling member. Access is per member, not per project: each member joins on their own and is invited as a read-only collaborator of the mirror. action "status" reports your state (not_connected / eligible / invited / joined / not_permitted / unavailable) with the repo URL once invited. action "join" sends the invitation; it needs a linked GitHub account (link_github), a plan that includes the source repository (Builder and up), the download_source capability, and YOUR acceptance of the GitHub addendum — if that is missing it answers GITHUB_ADDENDUM_CONSENT_REQUIRED: show the human the addendum with get_legal_status, record their acceptance with record_legal_consent (source github_delivery), then join again. A successful join usually leaves you "invited": the repository opens only after the human accepts the invitation on GitHub, within 7 days. action "leave" removes you from the mirror (a pending invitation is withdrawn too); it is reversible by joining again. get_docs(doc:"repo") gives the repository URL but the URL alone does not grant access.

action.description: status = read your participation; join = get invited as a read-only collaborator; leave = remove yourself (reversible).

tools.name: list_invoices
tools.description: List a project's billing history, newest first: one row per issued invoice with its total, status and receipt URL. The rows carry NO line breakdown, so this cannot tell you what any single component cost — for usage beyond the plan's included API calls and storage, read overage_amount in a preview_plan_change response, or the invoice.lines with their line_kind in the response from change_plan, cancel_subscription or purchase_tokens. Owner only. Amounts are Stripe minor units paired with a currency code, so do not assume two decimal places and do not reformat them. status is one of paid, open, void or uncollectible — uncollectible means the PAYMENT FAILED and the user needs to know about it, while void means the invoice was cancelled and is not owed. A refund does NOT change an invoice's status: check the refunded object instead, which is present only when a refund exists.

tools.name: list_members
tools.description: List a project's members, pending invites and seat requests. Seats are a billing unit, so this is where you find out WHO is occupying them when get_plan reports the seat bucket as full. Seat accounting: available = capacity − active members − open pending invites, meaning an invite that nobody has accepted yet still holds a seat. That same occupancy figure decides the next renewal — any add-on seat still empty then is removed automatically and drops off the bill. A member whose seat_status is "waiting" has no seat and therefore no access, but that resolves itself: waiting members are invited automatically as soon as seats are added, so never re-invite them by hand. seat_requests is only populated for the owner and comes back empty for an admin, so an empty list does not prove there are no pending requests; the owner resolves them with resolve_seat_request. Use preview_seats to price more seats. This list is also where the ids for acting on people come from: members[].id (a user UUID) is what manage_member takes to change a role, change a seat or remove someone, and invites[].id (an integer) is what manage_invite takes to cancel or resend an invitation.

tools.name: preview_seats
tools.description: Price out adding seats to a project before buying any. This has no side effects and charges nothing — it is the read-only counterpart of purchase_seats_and_invite. additional_seats is a DELTA (how many to add), not a total; set_seats takes an absolute total instead, so do not pass the same number to both. Returns the recurring add, the amount due today, and the next period's figure, all as minor units with a currency code — never compute these yourself, the proration comes from Stripe. prorated_now IS THE AMOUNT THE CARD WOULD BE CHARGED TODAY: extra seats live on their own monthly seat subscription and an increase is invoiced immediately, so buying is not deferred to the next invoice. creates_seat_subscription=true means this would be the project's first seat subscription, whose cycle is aligned to the plan's billing day — the first invoice only covers the days up to that date, so the figure can be small (Stripe carries amounts under about half a unit of currency to the next invoice rather than charging the card). next_invoice_date is the seat subscription's next billing date, which is the plan's billing day even on a yearly plan. Seats bought ahead of the people who will fill them do not last: at each renewal the subscription is shrunk to max(the plan's included seats, seats that are assigned or invited), so an empty seat stops renewing and leaves the bill. Only per-seat plans (pro, business) can add seats. Owner only. See list_members for who currently occupies the seats.

additional_seats.description: How many seats to ADD on top of the current total (a delta, minimum 1).

tools.name: get_billing_portal_url
tools.description: Create a one-time link to the billing portal, where a human can change the payment method, read past invoices, and manage or resume a subscription. This tool RETURNS A LINK AND NOTHING ELSE — it does not change any billing state, and receiving a URL is not the action succeeding. Give the link to the user and let them finish it in a browser. Resuming a subscription whose cancellation is scheduled has no API and can only be done here. The session expires, so fetch a fresh link each time rather than reusing an old one. Owner only.

tools.name: get_upgrade_url
tools.description: Get the link to a project's plan page in the web console. The browser is REQUIRED for exactly one transition: a Sandbox project's FIRST paid subscription, which goes through a hosted checkout that has no API — that is the case for this link. A project that already has a subscription does not need it: upgrade, downgrade or change interval with change_plan (priced by preview_plan_change), cancel with cancel_subscription, revert a pending change with withdraw_scheduled_plan_change. So when an action was refused for plan reasons (PLAN_UPGRADE_REQUIRED, PLAN_NO_SEATS, a plan-gated artifact), check get_plan first: plan.code=sandbox means hand the user this link, anything else means change_plan. A paid subscription that is PAST DUE (get_plan is_past_due — a payment failed and Stripe is still retrying it) keeps its paid plan code; do NOT hand that user this link, because a new checkout would open a second subscription — the fix is updating the card in the billing portal (get_billing_portal_url), after which the retried payment settles and the subscription is active again. This composes a URL locally and does not call the backend, so it always succeeds and proves nothing about the project's state.

tools.name: set_seats
tools.description: Set the TOTAL number of seats on a project's subscription. WARNING — seats is an ABSOLUTE TOTAL, not an amount to add. preview_seats takes a delta instead, so passing that delta here silently buys far more seats than intended: to go from 2 seats to 3, pass seats=3, not seats=1. RAISING THE TOTAL CHARGES THE CARD NOW. Extra seats live on their own monthly seat subscription, separate from the base plan (a yearly plan still bills seats monthly), and an increase is invoiced immediately for the rest of that seat period — there is no free trial on seats, so this charges even while the base plan is still in its trial. If no seat subscription exists yet the backend creates one and aligns its cycle to the plan's billing day, so the first invoice only covers the days up to that date and can be small. Lowering the total is scheduled for the next SEAT cycle (which is monthly even on a yearly plan) and never refunds the current one. Price it with preview_seats and read the current total from get_plan before calling. Seats do not persist just by being paid for: at each renewal the subscription is automatically shrunk to max(the plan's included seats, seats that are assigned or invited), so a seat that no member holds and no open invite reserves does not renew, drops off the bill, and the owner is emailed about it. Buying seats ahead of the people who will fill them is therefore not durable — buy them alongside the invites (purchase_seats_and_invite does both in one step). You must pass confirm=true. Only per-seat plans (pro, business) support this, the total cannot go below the plan's included seats, and it is owner only.

seats.description: The TOTAL seat count the subscription should have — an absolute value, not a delta. Includes the seats already paid for.

confirm.description: Must be true. Raising the total charges the owner's card TODAY for the rest of the seat period; show them preview_seats prorated_now first.

tools.name: purchase_seats_and_invite
tools.description: Buy additional seats and invite people in one step. THE SEATS ARE CHARGED TO THE CARD NOW: extra seats live on their own monthly subscription, separate from the base plan, and an increase is invoiced immediately for the rest of that seat period — there is no free trial on seats, so this charges even while the base plan is still in its trial. Price it with preview_seats first (prorated_now is the amount due today) and confirm the number with the user. additional_seats is a DELTA (how many to add), matching preview_seats; set_seats is the one that takes an absolute total. THERE IS NO PARTIAL ROLLBACK: if the seats are added but the invites then fail (someone else took the seats concurrently), THE SEATS ARE KEPT AND STILL BILLED — re-run list_members before retrying so you do not add them twice. Note that an open invite reserves a seat before anyone accepts it, so you may need fewer new seats than there are emails. Seats and invites belong together: at each renewal the subscription is automatically shrunk to max(the plan's included seats, seats that are assigned or invited), so a seat nobody holds and no open invite reserves does not renew and drops off the bill, with an email to the owner. That is why this tool buys and invites in one step — buying seats ahead of the people who will fill them does not stick. Anyone who ends up waiting for a seat is invited automatically once one frees up, so do not re-invite them by hand. You must pass confirm=true. Owner only, and only on per-seat plans (pro, business); an admin should use create_seat_request instead.

additional_seats.description: How many seats to ADD (a delta, not a total). Price it with preview_seats first.

emails.description: Every email to invite, including the ones that fit in seats the project already has free.

role.description: Project role to grant. editor: create and edit, but cannot deploy. operator: deploy, reboot and restore backups, but cannot manage members or billing. admin: everything an editor and an operator can do, plus member and billing management. Owner cannot be granted here. A role can be changed afterwards with manage_member, but the invite consumes a paid seat either way, so pick deliberately.

confirm.description: Must be true. This charges the owner's card today for the added seats.

tools.name: cancel_subscription
tools.description: End a project's subscription. A cancellation is always SCHEDULED, never applied on the spot: it takes effect at the end of the current billing period, the project keeps working on its plan until then, nothing is charged today, there is NO REFUND for the remaining time, and it can be reversed before that date with withdraw_scheduled_plan_change (the billing portal, via get_billing_portal_url, is the fallback route). A FREE TRIAL IS NOT AN EXCEPTION: cancelling during the trial takes effect at the trial end, the trial keeps running until then, no plan fee is charged after it, and it can be withdrawn the same way. So there is nothing to gain by waiting for the trial to end before cancelling — the first plan charge falls on the trial end, and a cancellation made after it comes too late to avoid that charge. What can still be billed is usage: API-call and database overage from the final window (the trial window included) is raised on its own invoice when the subscription ends, and a failed payment there does not stop the cancellation. The response carries cancel_at, the date the cancellation lands (current_period_end is the same value), ends_trial, which is always false, and during_trial, which says whether the subscription was in its free trial when it was cancelled (null when this call could not tell). preview_plan_change with plan_code=sandbox shows the same date beforehand as effective_at without changing anything. Cancelling also silently DROPS any scheduled plan change or seat reduction — get_plan plan.scheduled_change will read null afterwards — and ends the separate monthly seat subscription at the same date. Once it takes effect the project drops to the single-seat free Sandbox plan and loses everything the plan granted: source access, deployment and the higher allowances. This is not only the owner's loss — every member beyond that one seat is demoted, so TEAMMATES LOSE ACCESS TO THE PROJECT, not just the paid features. Check list_members for who that affects before confirming. You must pass confirm=true, and only after the user has explicitly asked to cancel. Calling it twice is harmless — it just reports the existing state. reason_code and reason_text are optional and only for a reason the user actually gave. Owner only. Downgrading to a cheaper paid plan instead is change_plan.

confirm.description: Must be true. Nothing is charged today, and the cancellation stays reversible until it lands — at the end of the billing period, or at the trial end during a free trial — via withdraw_scheduled_plan_change or the billing portal.

reason_code.description: Why the user is cancelling, if they said. Optional — omit rather than guess; it is stored for product analytics and changes nothing about the cancellation.

reason_text.description: Free-text detail in the user's words (max 1000 chars). Optional. If given without reason_code, reason_code defaults to "other" — the backend discards text that has no code.

tools.name: preview_plan_change
tools.description: Price a plan change before making it: returns what the owner would be charged TODAY for moving this project to plan_code (and optionally another billing interval), without changing anything. Read mode first. immediate means the change would be applied and charged right now, and only then are the amount fields present — amount_due_now is the figure to show the user; plan_amount is the recurring price from the next period and is NOT part of today's charge; anchor_reset=true means the billing period restarts today. deferred means the change would be scheduled for the end of the current period with nothing charged now (downgrades, interval shortening, and moves that drop a capability — see change_plan on why a MORE expensive plan can land here). cancel means plan_code=sandbox would cancel (use cancel_subscription for that): nothing is due today and effective_at is when the cancellation would land — the period end, or the trial end during a free trial — and same means it is already the current plan (see withdraw_scheduled_plan_change). Under the current pricing policy every immediate change re-anchors the billing period, and Stripe refuses to pin a calculation instant across an anchor reset, so proration_date comes back null and amount_locked false for an immediate change — there is normally nothing to pass to change_plan and the amount is recomputed at confirmation time. Preview again immediately before confirming and read the invoice change_plan returns for what was actually billed. AMOUNTS ARE PRE-TAX EXCEPT amount_due_now. The summary figures (plan_amount, proration_charge, proration_credit, pending_items, plan_amount_due_now) and every line amount are pre-tax, and the identity proration_charge + proration_credit + pending_items matches the plan invoice's SUBTOTAL, not the charge; each entry in invoices then carries subtotal, tax, total and taxes, and the card is billed amount_due_now, which is post-tax and net of any customer credit. For a customer in a country with VAT the pre-tax figures understate the charge by the whole tax, so quote amount_due_now and nothing else. pending_items splits further into overage_amount (usage beyond the plan's included API calls and database storage, in the closing window) and other_pending; label that portion with overage_amount rather than with overage.amount. The summary describes the PLAN invoice only: when a seat subscription is settled alongside, invoices lists one entry per Stripe invoice and the top-level amount_due_now is their sum — do not check it against the plan-only arithmetic. Judge that by invoices having more than one entry, not by separate_invoices, which is always true (a design statement that seats and plan can never share an invoice, not a per-response signal). ends_trial=true is an irreversible fact worth surfacing before anything else: the free trial ends today and the new plan is charged in full. trial_end is set instead when this change would START a trial (nothing due today). Amounts are Stripe minor units in the currency named by the currency field — do not assume two decimal places. Owner only; a Sandbox project has no subscription to change and is refused — its first subscription starts in the browser via get_upgrade_url. See get_plan for the current plan and is_trialing, and preview_seats for seat pricing.

plan_code.description: Target plan. sandbox previews a cancellation (mode=cancel) — actually cancelling goes through cancel_subscription.

interval.description: Target billing interval. Omit to keep the current interval — that is what you want for a plain tier change.

tools.name: change_plan
tools.description: Change a project's subscription plan or billing interval. THIS TOOL CAN CHARGE THE CARD RIGHT NOW: an upgrade is applied immediately and the prorated difference is invoiced on the spot. A downgrade is scheduled for the end of the current period with no refund, and at rollover the project loses whatever the new plan does not include: moving to a plan without seats (starter, builder) REMOVES EVERY MEMBER EXCEPT THE OWNER, so check list_members first. WHICH DIRECTION A MOVE COUNTS AS IS DECIDED BY FEATURES, NOT PRICE: a target plan that drops a capability the current plan has is a downgrade even when it costs more, so Pro or Business to Builder is scheduled for the period end and RECLAIMS THE LIVE DEPLOYMENT when it lands, despite being the pricier plan. Builder to Pro or Business is a superset and applies at once. Raising the plan and shortening the interval in one call is accepted and lands together at the end of the paid term. Always call preview_plan_change first and show the user its amount_due_now (or that nothing is charged now); pass its proration_date back here when the preview returned one, though under the current pricing policy an immediate change re-anchors the period and the preview normally returns null. amount_due_now is post-tax; the line amounts and the proration summary are pre-tax, so never quote a line total as the charge. Read charged_now in the result rather than inferring payment from status: the invoice is raised first and paid second, and a declined card can leave it open under Stripe's retry process instead of failing this call. If the subscription is in its free trial (get_plan is_trialing, which the raw status hides), ANY change here ends the trial immediately and charges the new plan in full today; the result reports ends_trial. Two transitions are deliberately not accepted — plan_code=sandbox (that is cancelling; use cancel_subscription, which carries the right warnings) and re-selecting the current plan (that is a withdrawal; use withdraw_scheduled_plan_change). A Sandbox project has no subscription to change: its first paid subscription is started by the user in the browser via get_upgrade_url. Owner only. In the result, plan_code and interval are the plan AFTER the call, scheduled_change holds a deferred target, and invoice is the invoice this change actually raised.

plan_code.description: Target plan (starter, builder, pro, business). sandbox is not accepted here — cancelling is cancel_subscription.

interval.description: Target billing interval. Omit to keep the current interval. month→year is applied and charged immediately; year→month is scheduled for the end of the prepaid term, as is a tier rise combined with a shortening.

proration_date.description: The proration_date from the preview_plan_change response you showed the user, passed straight back, when the preview returned one. Under the current pricing policy every immediate change re-anchors the billing period and Stripe refuses to pin a calculation instant across an anchor reset, so the preview normally returns null with amount_locked=false and there is nothing to pass — that is expected, not a fault. When a value IS returned, passing it back computes the charge from the same instant as the quote. A value that has gone stale (over 30 minutes old, or the billing period or trial state moved) is refused with PLAN_CHANGE_PREVIEW_STALE and nothing changes. Either way, report invoice.amount_due_now from this tool's response as the amount actually billed.

confirm.description: Must be true, and only after the user has seen the preview_plan_change result. An upgrade charges the card immediately; a downgrade is irreversible at rollover and can remove members and reclaim a deployment; a change during a free trial ends the trial for good.

tools.name: withdraw_scheduled_plan_change
tools.description: Undo a pending subscription change so the project simply keeps its current plan: drops a scheduled downgrade or interval change, and reverses an end-of-period cancellation made with cancel_subscription — including one made during a free trial, which is scheduled for the trial end. Reversing a cancellation means the subscription renews again and billing resumes from the next period; during a free trial it means the trial simply continues, nothing is charged today, and the plan's first charge falls on the trial end. Either way money is billed again later, which is why confirm=true is required. Check get_plan first — plan.scheduled_change shows a pending change and plan.status=canceled a pending cancellation. If neither is present there is nothing to withdraw and the tool reports withdrawn=false without an error. It sends the project's CURRENT plan code back to the backend and never touches the billing interval, so unlike change_plan it cannot accidentally schedule a new change. Owner only.

confirm.description: Must be true. Withdrawing a cancellation makes the subscription renew and bill again from the next period — for a cancellation made during a free trial, from the trial end, when the plan is charged for the first time.

tools.name: redeem_coupon
tools.description: Register a promo code from the BackendX pre-signup campaign email on the current account. One code per account and one account per code; case and surrounding whitespace are ignored. Registering does NOT apply the benefit: the coupon is held on the account and attaches automatically to the next Pro MONTHLY checkout, which the user completes in the browser (get_upgrade_url) — it never applies to yearly billing or to other plans. status=redeemed means the code was just attached; already_redeemed only means this account already holds it, not that the benefit is still available — read held (derived from claimed, used and expires_at) in the response, or get_account later. The backend checks account eligibility before it looks at the code, so an ineligible account is told so without learning whether the code exists. Not a purchase — no confirm needed.

code.description: The promo code from the campaign email.

tools.name: create_seat_request
tools.description: Invite people as an admin when the project does not have enough seats: the ones that fit in free seats are invited immediately, and the rest are queued as a single seat request for the OWNER to approve. This is the admin's route — only the owner can buy seats, so purchase_seats_and_invite returns NOT_PROJECT_OWNER for anyone else. Nothing is charged here; the seats are only bought if and when the owner approves (resolve_seat_request). Pass every email you want on the project, not just the ones you expect to overflow — the backend recalculates free capacity itself and splits the list. If capacity turns out to be sufficient, everyone is invited and seat_request comes back null, which is success rather than a failure. The owner is emailed about a queued request, and it expires on its own after about two weeks if nobody acts on it. Requires an admin role; see list_members for the current occupancy.

emails.description: Every email to invite, including the ones that fit in seats the project already has free. Addresses that are already members or already invited are reported back under skipped rather than failing the call.

role.description: Project role to grant. editor: create and edit, but cannot deploy. operator: deploy, reboot and restore backups, but cannot manage members or billing. admin: everything an editor and an operator can do, plus member and billing management. Owner cannot be granted here. A role can be changed afterwards with manage_member, but the invite consumes a paid seat either way, so pick deliberately.

requested_seats.description: How many seats you believe are short. Advisory only — the backend recalculates from live capacity and its own number wins, so omitting this is fine.

tools.name: resolve_seat_request
tools.description: Approve or reject a seat request an admin queued with create_seat_request. Owner only — see list_members for the pending requests and their ids. APPROVING BUYS SEATS AND CHARGES THE CARD NOW: it adds exactly the requested number to the subscription, invoices them immediately on the separate monthly seat subscription, and sends the waiting invites. Approve only when the user has said so, and price it with preview_seats first (prorated_now is the amount due today). Rejecting costs nothing and sends no invites. Both actions are one-way — there is no tool to un-approve — but approving twice is safe: the backend converges on the existing approval instead of buying again. A request that was already rejected or has expired cannot be approved afterwards. approve requires confirm=true.

request_id.description: Seat request id (an integer, from list_members)

action.description: approve: buy the requested seats and send the waiting invites — this charges the owner's card today. reject: decline the request; no seats, no invites, no charge.

confirm.description: Required (true) for approve, since it charges the owner's card today for the seats. Ignored for reject.

tools.name: get_role_matrix
tools.description: Read this project's role definitions: which capability each role carries, and which capabilities are owner-only. CALL THIS AFTER A PERMISSION REFUSAL from any member, invite, seat or share tool — those refusals come back with no reason attached, because the backend answers a permission failure with an empty body, so this is the only way to find out which role would actually have worked. It matters most on a project that defines custom roles, where the usual "you need to be an admin" advice can simply be wrong. A capability listed under reserved_capabilities can never be delegated to any role, custom ones included, so an action needing one always means "ask the owner" and no role change will help. Read-only and free — it changes nothing. Any member holding a seat can call it; a refusal here means you have no seat on this project rather than too low a role.

tools.name: manage_invite
tools.description: Send, cancel or resend project invitations. Requires an admin or owner role. Nothing is charged here and no card is touched: an invite RESERVES one of the seats the project already has at the moment it is sent, and cancelling gives that seat slot straight back. That is why a send can be refused for lack of seats even though it costs nothing — buying the missing seats is a separate step (purchase_seats_and_invite for the owner, create_seat_request for an admin). Sending is a batch: an address that is already a member or already holds an open invite is reported under skipped instead of failing the call, so ALWAYS read invites and skipped separately — a successful call can still have invited nobody. Invalid addresses or a seat shortage reject the whole batch instead, leaving nothing sent. Invites expire on their own after about a week, and cancel and resend both take the integer invites[].id from list_members, not a member UUID.

action.description: send: email one or more people an invitation, reserving a seat for each (needs emails and role). cancel: revoke a pending invitation and free the seat it was holding (needs invite_id). resend: email the same invitation again, subject to a server-side cooldown (needs invite_id).

emails.description: action="send" only. Every address to invite. Addresses that are already members or already invited come back under skipped rather than failing the call, so passing the full list is safe.

role.description: action="send" only. Project role to grant. editor: create and edit, but cannot deploy. operator: deploy, reboot and restore backups, but cannot manage members or billing. admin: everything an editor and an operator can do, plus member and billing management. Owner cannot be granted here. A role can be changed afterwards with manage_member, but the invite consumes a paid seat either way, so pick deliberately.

invite_id.description: action="cancel" and action="resend" only. The integer id of a pending invite, from invites[].id in list_members. This is NOT a member UUID.

tools.name: manage_member
tools.description: Change an existing member's role, change which seat state they hold, or remove them from the project. Requires an admin or owner role. Identify the person with member_user_uuid, which is members[].id from list_members — a user UUID, never the integer id of an invite or a seat request. Two rows in that list can never be targeted here: the owner (move ownership with transfer_ownership instead) and yourself (use leave_project). Removing someone frees the seat they occupied for somebody else but does NOT reduce the subscription or refund anything — the bill only shrinks when the seat count itself is lowered (set_seats) or at renewal. Changing a role is reversible and costs nothing; removing is not reversible, and getting back in needs a fresh invitation against a seat. If this is refused for a permission reason, get_role_matrix says which role would have worked, which matters on projects that define their own roles.

member_user_uuid.description: The member's user UUID — members[].id from list_members. Not an invite id and not a seat-request id.

action.description: change_role: give the member a different role (reversible, free). remove: delete their membership entirely, freeing their seat for someone else but changing nothing on the bill. change_seat: move them between holding a seat and not holding one, without ending their membership.

role.description: action="change_role" only. The preset roles are admin, editor, operator, document_viewer, deployment_monitor, and a project may define custom roles on top of those — get_role_matrix lists what this project actually accepts and what each role can do. Owner cannot be granted here; use transfer_ownership. There is no last-admin rule: demoting the only admin, yourself included, is allowed.

seat_status.description: action="change_seat" only. active: give them a paid seat and full access (needs a free seat to exist). waiting: take the seat back immediately — they stay a member but lose access until a seat is given again. pending_removal: let them keep working until the end of the paid period, then drop to no seat automatically; this needs an active subscription to have a period end to schedule against.

confirm.description: Required (true) for action="remove", and for action="change_seat" when seat_status is waiting or pending_removal — each of those takes someone's access away. Not needed for a role change or for granting a seat.

tools.name: transfer_ownership
tools.description: Hand this project over to another member. THIS IS ONE-WAY FOR THE CALLER: the moment it succeeds the current owner becomes a plain admin and only the NEW owner can ever transfer it back, so a mistake cannot be undone without that person's cooperation. Ownership is the billing anchor — the new owner is who the subscription belongs to, and the outgoing owner loses the right to buy seats, manage billing and delete the project while keeping everything an admin can do. The target must already be a member with an accepted invitation; a pending invite is not enough, so check members[].id in list_members rather than the invites list. Only the current owner can call this and no role change grants it to anyone else — it is a reserved capability. Requires confirm=true.

new_owner_user_uuid.description: The user UUID of the member who becomes the owner — members[].id from list_members. They must already be a member; somebody with a pending invitation cannot receive ownership.

confirm.description: Required (true). Transferring demotes the caller to admin and only the new owner can transfer it back, so the user has to say so explicitly.

tools.name: leave_project
tools.description: Leave a project you are a member of. This acts on YOU, not on somebody else — removing another person is manage_member(action="remove"). Access ends immediately and getting back in needs a fresh invitation from someone who can still manage members, so it is not something to do speculatively. No particular role is needed and no seat is needed either: a member who is waiting for a seat can still leave. Two people cannot: the owner has to hand the project over first (transfer_ownership), and an admin has to stop being an admin first — manage_member(action="change_role") on their own row does it, and there is no last-admin rule standing in the way, so nobody has to be promoted first. Leaving frees the seat you occupied for someone else but changes nothing about what the project pays. Requires confirm=true.

confirm.description: Required (true). Leaving ends your own access immediately and only someone still on the project can invite you back.

tools.name: claim_invite
tools.description: Accept a project invitation and become a member, using the token from the invitation email. This is the only way in: there is no API that lists invitations waiting for you, so the user has to bring the link from their inbox — ask them to paste the whole invite URL, this tool pulls the token out of it. The account that accepts is whoever is authenticated here, and that deliberately does not have to be the address the invitation was sent to, so an invitation to a work address can be accepted by an account created with a personal one. Accepting is safe to repeat: if you are already a member the call still reports success rather than an error. What is NOT repeatable is the invitation — every accepted call marks it used, including the already-a-member one, so claiming a link that was addressed to somebody else kills it and they have to be invited again. Only ever pass a link the user says is theirs. It costs nothing — the seat was reserved when the invitation was sent. Whether you get access right away depends on whether that seat is still free; if it is not, you join as a member without a seat and are picked up automatically once one is. This is the one project tool that takes no project_uuid: the token decides which project.

token.description: The invitation token, or the whole invite URL from the email — a link like https://.../invite?token=… works as-is, the token is extracted from it.

tools.name: manage_share_link
tools.description: List, publish or revoke the links that expose this project's documents at a fetchable URL. THIS IS ALSO HOW A LINK IS TAKEN BACK: the public URL that get_api_clipboard(link=true) hands out is one of these rows, so it shows up under action="list" and revoking it there is the only way to invalidate it — nothing else can. Revoking kills that URL for good; a later get_api_clipboard(link=true) mints a brand new one rather than reviving it. Publishing a public link means anyone holding the URL can read that document with no login at all, which is the point when the link is going to an AI tool that can fetch URLs, and a real exposure otherwise — so it needs confirm=true. A private link is the opposite and is usually a mistake here: fetching it still demands a logged-in account with permission on this project, so no external tool can read it. Listing is open to any member with a seat; publishing and revoking need the owner, admin or editor role.

action.description: list: show every live share link on this project, including the one behind get_api_clipboard(link=true). create: publish a new link (needs artifact_type and visibility). revoke: invalidate one permanently (needs share_id from list).

artifact_type.description: action="create" only. api_doc: the API documentation, Markdown with the OpenAPI spec included. integration_prompt: a ready-to-follow instruction set for building a client against this backend. srs: the requirements document as JSON. architecture: the architecture as JSON. api_doc_frontend: the API documentation without the admin-only endpoints (what get_api_clipboard(audience="frontend", link=true) publishes). api_doc_public: the public-scope API documentation the welcome page of the deployed app points its AI prompt at. The document has to exist already — run the pipeline first if it does not (wait_for_pipeline).

visibility.description: action="create" only. public: anyone with the URL reads it, no login — this is the only setting an outside tool can actually use, and it needs confirm=true. private: the URL still demands a logged-in account with permission on this project, so it is useless for handing to an external tool and only makes sense for a teammate who is already a member.

include_deployed_base_url.description: action="create" only. Bake the live deployment's base URL into what the link serves, so a generated client points at the real host instead of a placeholder. Recorded when the link is minted, but the URL itself is looked up on each fetch, so a link made before the deployment exists starts carrying the real host once it does.

expires_at.description: action="create" only. ISO-8601 timestamp after which the link stops working. Omit for a link that never expires on its own — it then lives until it is revoked here.

share_id.description: action="revoke" only. The integer id of the link, from action="list".

confirm.description: Required (true) to create a link with visibility="public", since that publishes the document at a URL anyone can read without logging in. Not needed for listing, revoking, or a private link.
